930.text: In Col.3.15, the adjective 'thankful' (G2170) is commanded in the immediate context of M33 (peace, G1515) ruling in the heart and M47 (heart, G2588) as the site where that peace and thankfulness reside -- thankfulness here is the disposition that accompanies and issues from Christ's peace governing the heart, presented as a fitting response to the unity of the one body. No prior context exists for this verse; this is the first pass.

943.text: In Col.3.15 the occurrence of G2170 sits squarely within the base gloss 'grateful, thankful' with no notable divergence from its ordinary sense; it is the word's only NT occurrence, so no cross-occurrence comparison is possible.

1115.text: In 1Chr.16.4, thanksgiving (H3034) is grouped with invocation (M81, H2142) and praise (M08/M16/M22, H1984B) as the threefold liturgical service assigned to the Levites -- thanksgiving occupies the middle term between remembering/invoking God and praising him, marking it as the responsive acknowledgment phase of worship.

1125.text: In 1Chr.16.4 the Levites, appointed by David (implied party), initiate the thanksgiving-operation directed toward the Lord, God of Israel, before the ark.

1240.text: Col.3.15's imperatival 'be thankful' uses G2170 in its standard NT sense (grateful, mindful of benefits) with no notable divergence; this is in fact the term's only NT occurrence, so no comparison across multiple occurrences is possible.

1249.text: Building on the prior finding (thankfulness accompanying Christ's peace, M33, ruling the heart, M47): from thankfulness's own vantage, being commanded as the concluding imperative of the verse shows it functioning as the capstone disposition that should characterize the 'one body' called to peace -- thankfulness here is the fitting communal response that completes and stabilizes the peace-governed, united heart just described.

1349.text: In 1Chr.16.4 the infinitive construct form matches the standard institutional 'to thank' sense with no shift beyond the base gloss.

1359.text: Building on the prior finding of thanksgiving as the middle term between invocation and praise: from thanksgiving's own vantage, it is the pivot that requires both a prior remembering (invocation, M81) and gives rise to an ensuing acclamation (praise, M08/M16/M22) -- structurally it cannot stand alone in this triad, marking it as transitional rather than terminal.

1369.text: Role-T3 operation 'appointed' (H5414H) is initiated by an unnamed royal/administrative subject (David, per context) directed toward the Levites, assigning them the subsequent acts of invoking, thanking (H3034), and praising the Lord -- thanksgiving is the assigned task-object of the appointing operation.

1634.text: In Col.3.15 'thankful' sits within the base gloss of grateful disposition; this is the term's sole NT occurrence, so no other NT occurrence exists for comparison, and the sense here matches the classical 'grateful, thankful' sense directly with no notable divergence.

1643.text: Building on the prior finding (thankfulness as capstone disposition completing the peace-governed united heart): from thankfulness's own vantage in Col.3.15, its adjectival/state form (rather than a verb of acting) shows it functioning as the abiding character-quality that should permanently mark the heart already ruled by M33 (peace) and unified in M47 (heart)/one body, distinguishing it from a punctual act of thanking and casting it instead as the stable disposition completing that peace-governed state.

1644.text: G2170 in Col.3.15 is an adjective describing a commanded disposition, not itself an operation word; the role-T3 operation in this verse is 'rule' (G1018, M72), initiated by the peace of Christ and directed toward 'your hearts' -- thankfulness is the resulting complementary disposition rather than an operation with its own initiator/target relation.

1743.text: Building on the prior finding of thanksgiving as pivot between invocation (M81) and praise (M08/M16/M22): this vantage adds that thanksgiving is the only one of the three liturgical terms carried by a plain infinitive construct parallel to the others, showing it was conceived by the text as co-equal in liturgical rank with invocation and praise, not subordinate.

1753.text: In 1Chr.16.4 H3034 ('thank') carries only M49, not role-T3; the role-T3 operation present is 'praise' (H1984B), initiated by the appointed Levites and directed toward the Lord God of Israel -- H3034 is not itself the operation-tagged word in this verse.

2968.text: G2170 is the only member strong in this subgroup, so there is no second member strong within C_thankful_disposition against which to synergise similarity or divergence -- the cross-strong-comparison task this stage exists for has no internal partner here; any comparison of disposition-vs-act belongs to the wider cluster M49 (e.g. against G2168) rather than within this single-member subgroup.

2969.text: G2170's full corpus-wide occurrence list is exactly one verse (Col.3.15); there is no internal occurrence-group variation to compare (no differing stems, voices, or renderings across occurrences) -- the strong's entire subgroup-level profile is defined by this single instance alone.

2970.text: The morph code A-NPM (adjective, nominative plural masculine) shows the subject IS thankful (a predicated state of being) rather than performing, having-done-to, or causing an action -- there is no verbal stem/voice variation to check since this strong is never verbal in the NT; its single occurrence confirms the adjectival form is used exclusively to name a possessed quality, consistent with its Stage 1 grammatical observations (M0.5.2) and requiring no further voice-based distinction within the subgroup.

2971.text: LSJ's classical range for eucharistos shows three distinguishable candidate senses that could each color Col.3.15's imperative differently: (1) 'agreeable, pleasing' (of a person's manner or speech toward others), (2) 'grateful, mindful of benefits, thankful' (the standard NT/Mounce gloss, inward disposition toward a benefactor), and (3) 'beneficent' (an outward-facing generosity, used as a divine/royal epithet). Since this subgroup has only the one occurrence, the command 'be thankful' in Col.3.15 could plausibly be read as primarily sense (2) per Mounce/strong_meaning_tree, but the LSJ range leaves open a minor secondary reading that the disposition commanded also makes the person 'agreeable/pleasing' to others in the one body, not merely inwardly grateful toward God.

2972.text: Across its full occurrence list H8426 clusters into three recurring realizations of one lexeme: (1) the concrete thank-offering sacrifice (Lev.7.12 x2, Lev.7.13, Lev.7.15, Lev.22.29, Ps.50.14, Ps.50.23, Ps.107.22, Ps.116.17, Amos.4.5, Jonah.2.9, 2Chr.29.31 x2, 2Chr.33.16, Jer.17.26, Jer.33.11), (2) the vocal/manner accompaniment of praise, 'with/in thanksgiving' (Ps.69.30, Ps.26.7, Ps.95.2, Ps.100.4, Ps.147.7, Isa.51.3), and (3) the institutional thanksgiving choir/procession/company (Neh.12.27, Neh.12.31, Neh.12.38, Neh.12.40, Ps.42.4). A fourth, rarer sense realizes it as verbal confession (Josh.7.19, Ezra.10.11). This is a single strong showing internally the full sense-range attributed to the subgroup label (hymn, choir, offering) without needing a second member strong to supply any of these senses.

3089.text: In Col.3.15, being 'thankful' reveals a settled belief that peace, unity, and benefit received all trace back to Christ -- the command to be thankful presupposes the person perceives their calling into 'one body' under Christ's peace as a genuine benefit meriting an ongoing grateful response, not merely a passing feeling.

3090.text: With only one occurrence of G2170 in the corpus, no sequential pattern of the characteristic preceding or following a judgement/belief can be established; the single instance shows the command following a stated belief (Christ's peace ruling, one-body calling) but this could be resolvable with cross-reference to the broader M49 cluster's verbal-thanksgiving occurrences (G2168), which lies outside this subgroup's own evidence.

3091.text: There is no explicit future-fullness orientation in G2170's single occurrence; the command 'be thankful' addresses a present, ongoing disposition rather than a future state to be attained. No forward-looking telos language accompanies it in this verse.

3092.text: Only one occurrence exists, so no cross-verse consistency-versus-variation comparison of an immediate response can be made from this subgroup's own evidence alone.

3093.text: The evidence distinguishes disposition from act at the lexical level: G2170 (adjective) names a sustained, settled quality of being thankful, in contrast to G2168's verb-form naming the discrete, punctual act of giving thanks -- the sustained effect is the abiding character trait itself, not a repeatable action.

3094.text: The single occurrence gives no explicit before/after transformation narrative to assess reversibility; the imperative form assumes the disposition can be taken up (and by implication could lapse, since it is commanded rather than automatic), but this is inferential rather than evidenced directly.

3095.text: Only one context (Col.3.15) is evidenced for this strong, so no cross-context variation in mechanism can be shown; the mechanism here is a direct imperative command embedded in a body-unity/peace context.

3096.text: The characteristic's role reads as belonging to created/redeemed design rather than the fallen condition -- it is commanded as fitting identity for those 'called in one body' under Christ's peace, i.e., a mark of the renewed community rather than a remnant of fallenness.

3097.text: In Col.3.15 the characteristic is shown as a settled disposition (predicate adjective in an imperative, 'be thankful') rather than a transient emotional response; no explicit emotion-language or bodily-feeling language accompanies it directly, though it is set alongside the heart (G2588) as the site where Christ's peace rules, implying an inward, felt orientation without named affect-vocabulary.

3098.text: With only one occurrence, cross-verse consistency-versus-context-variation of the felt quality cannot be established from this subgroup's own evidence.

3099.text: Only one context is attested for G2170, so no variation by context, direction, or constitutional level can be demonstrated from this subgroup's evidence alone.

3100.text: Yes -- the characteristic operates through a directly communicative/speech-based mode: it is commanded ('be thankful') as an imperative addressed to the community, functioning as a verbal instruction establishing an identity marker rather than arising spontaneously.

3101.text: The inner condition for the characteristic to take hold rightly, per the verse context, is the heart being ruled by the peace of Christ and the awareness of being called into one body -- thankfulness is presented as the fitting disposition that arises from and completes that peace-governed, unified inner state.

3102.text: This subgroup's single verse (Col.3.15) gives the positive condition (peace of Christ ruling the heart) but does not itself state what blocks or distorts thankfulness; determining what resists or interferes with this disposition (e.g. surrounding vices in Colossians 3's list) would require adjacent-verse context beyond this subgroup's own evidence -- flagged for the synergy stage.

3103.text: The verse commands the disposition positively; it does not describe a case where the characteristic is present but fails to take hold, so the inner-being state of such a person is not evidenced in this subgroup's own material.

3104.text: The evidence shows the characteristic operating within an existing relational bond -- it is commanded specifically to those 'called in one body,' i.e. within the covenant community bound together by Christ's peace, rather than being addressed across relational distance or difference.

3105.text: The characteristic operates within a covenantal context -- it is commanded to those called into 'one body' in Christ; the single occurrence gives no evidence of it crossing covenantal boundaries to those outside that body.

3106.text: The relational scope includes those called into the one body under Christ's peace -- the command is addressed to the gathered community as an identity marker; the verse gives no explicit statement about whether or how it extends to those outside that body.

3107.text: The single occurrence of the adjectival 'thankful' disposition (versus the more frequent verbal act-form G2168 elsewhere) suggests that as a named, settled trait of the divine image it is rare in explicit lexical form but implied to be foundational -- it is commanded as a completing mark of the redeemed community's inner constitution, suggesting the trait's proper place is central to the renewed human person even though rarely named as a fixed quality.

3108.text: The inner posture required, per the verse, is a heart already ruled by the peace of Christ and mindful of its calling into the one body -- a receptive, unified, peace-governed heart is the posture that enables the human-to-God movement of gratitude.

3109.text: The human-to-God direction of thankfulness shows the person acknowledging Christ's peace and the benefit of the calling to one body as gifts to be received and recognized as such -- gratitude functions as a relational posture of dependence and acknowledgement toward the giver.

3110.text: Given the term's classical range including 'beneficent' as a divine/royal epithet (LSJ sense III) alongside the human sense 'grateful, thankful,' the aspect of divine likeness instantiated is the capacity to recognize, receive, and rightly respond to grace/favor -- mirroring, in creaturely form, the disposition of a God who is himself the source and giver of all good.

3111.text: The evidence points to this as primarily a creaturely analogue rather than a shared attribute in the same sense: humans are 'thankful' as grateful recipients of grace, while God is never described by this adjective as being grateful; the closest divine parallel (LSJ's 'beneficent' sense) shows God as the giver of benefit that occasions human thankfulness, not as one who is himself thankful in the same sense.

3112.text: Where thankfulness is present, per Col.3.15, it indicates the divine image is functioning rightly within the unified body -- the peace of Christ ruling the heart and the resulting gratitude together indicate a restored, rightly-ordered inner constitution reflecting God's design for the redeemed community; the verse does not evidence what its absence indicates.

3113.text: The characteristic engages the heart (G2588) level explicitly as the seat where Christ's peace rules and thankfulness is commanded to accompany it; no bodily-organ level is engaged in this verse -- the disposition is located at the inner/heart level with no direct body link evidenced, indicating depth at the affective-volitional center of the person rather than at any bodily expression.

3114.text: No body link is evidenced for G2170 in its sole occurrence; the disposition is located at the heart level with no reference to bodily expression or feedback in this verse.

3115.text: The movement evidenced is from an external source (the peace of Christ, ruling) into the heart, with thankfulness commanded as the fitting responsive disposition that settles there -- the sequence is Christ's peace acting upon/ruling the heart, and thankfulness following as the heart's own settled quality, rather than a movement from spirit to soul to body.

3116.text: The verse does not frame God directly extending the characteristic of thankfulness to the person as a gift; rather, thankfulness is a commanded human response to the benefit already given (calling into one body under Christ's ruling peace) -- so on the available evidence, the basis is responsive (a fitting human reply to what God has already done) rather than an unconditional bestowal of the trait itself.

3117.text: The verse's naming of thankfulness as a fitting response to Christ's peace and the calling to one body shows God's disposition toward the human person as fundamentally benefactive -- one who confers unity and peace as gifts warranting grateful acknowledgement, consistent with the classical sense of the root as denoting beneficence.

3118.text: The single occurrence gives no scenario of one person extending thankfulness to another (it is a divine-to-human/community-command context), so the inner conditions accompanying interpersonal extension of this characteristic are not evidenced in this subgroup's own material.

3119.text: Per the verse, a person must have received the peace of Christ ruling their heart and recognized their calling into one body before they can rightly be commanded to be thankful -- thankfulness presupposes prior reception of grace/unity as its ground.

3120.text: No interpersonal transmission scenario (one person's thankfulness reaching another) is evidenced in this subgroup's single occurrence, so inner conditions for uptake from another person cannot be established from this evidence alone.

3121.text: No case of a person failing to take up thankfulness offered by another is evidenced in this subgroup's sole verse; not determinable from this evidence.

3122.text: No adversarial activity or interference with the characteristic is evidenced anywhere in G2170's single occurrence; the verse presents thankfulness purely as a positive commanded disposition with no mention of opposition or spiritual conflict.

3123.text: No angelic mediation or ministry is evidenced in connection with G2170's single occurrence; the disposition is commanded directly by the apostolic instruction with Christ's peace as its stated ground, with no angelic intermediary role indicated.

3124.text: With only a single occurrence, no cross-verse comparison of single versus multiple origin, or contextual change in origin, can be established from this subgroup's own evidence.

3125.text: The heart (G2588) is the only inner faculty explicitly engaged in this verse, with no engagement of mind, conscience, or will named directly -- this narrow but central engagement indicates the characteristic's nature as an affective-volitional disposition seated at the heart, the governing center, rather than a cognitive or purely behavioral trait.

3126.text: G2170 is a disposition -- an adjective naming a settled quality/character trait ('thankful') rather than a discrete act, distinguishing it grammatically and semantically from the verb-form G2168 which names the act of giving thanks.

3127.text: The characteristic is simple in surface structure (a single adjective) but compound at the root level: eu- (well) + charis (grace/favor), combining the notion of favor received with a positive/well-disposed orientation toward it.

3128.text: No lexically supplied antonym (e.g. 'ungrateful') appears among this subgroup's sources; the structural opposite would be an unthankful or ungrateful disposition, but this is inferred rather than directly evidenced in the given material.

3129.text: By its placement in Col.3.15 alongside the peace of Christ ruling the heart, the characteristic implicitly excludes discord, ingratitude, and forgetfulness of benefit received -- it resists an inner state that fails to recognize unity and grace as gifts warranting response.

3130.text: The characteristic ends where the discrete verbal act of thanking (G2168) begins -- G2170 names the settled disposition/quality, not the punctual performed act; it is not the act of thanksgiving itself but the character trait underlying and motivating such acts.

3131.text: In Col.3.15, thankfulness co-occurs with peace (G1515, 'the peace of Christ') ruling the heart, and with the calling into 'one body' (unity) -- these are the only adjacent characteristics present in this subgroup's single occurrence, appearing together in the same verse.

3132.text: The co-occurrence of thankfulness with Christ's ruling peace and bodily unity shows this characteristic's place in the inner-being landscape as a capstone or completing disposition -- it does not stand alone but is presented as the fitting response that follows from and stabilizes a peace-governed, unified heart.

3133.text: In the single occurrence, thankfulness follows in sequence after the peace of Christ ruling the heart and the calling into one body -- the verse's own word order and logic present peace-ruling as prior ground and thankfulness as the resulting/accompanying disposition ('let peace rule... and be thankful').

3134.text: The sequence shown (peace ruling, then thankfulness commanded) reads as developmental/correlational rather than strictly causal in a mechanical sense -- thankfulness is presented as a fitting companion disposition that completes the peace-governed state, not as an inevitable automatic effect but as a further command building on the same footing.

3135.text: No other characteristic is shown as directly produced by thankfulness in this subgroup's evidence; the verse presents it as a terminal, capstone command rather than a generative source of further named traits.

3136.text: Yes -- thankfulness is shown as produced by or arising alongside the peace of Christ ruling the heart and the calling into one body; these prior realities are presented as the ground from which the commanded thankful disposition fittingly follows.

3137.text: No evidence in this subgroup shows thankfulness as a constituent element of another characteristic, or another characteristic as a constituent part of it; it stands as its own distinct disposition in the verse.

3138.text: The nearest adjacent characteristic is the verbal act of giving thanks (G2168, eucharisteo) within the wider M49 cluster; what distinguishes them is that G2170 names the settled disposition/quality of being thankful (adjective, state of being) while G2168 names the discrete performed act of giving thanks (verb, action) -- disposition versus act is the precise distinguishing line.

3139.text: The boundary between the disposition (G2170) and the act (G2168) is that the disposition is the underlying, ongoing character trait that may or may not be expressed in any given discrete act of thanksgiving -- overlap occurs because the disposition naturally issues in acts, but the disposition itself is not reducible to any single act or occasion of thanking.

3140.text: The distinction from the nearest neighbour (G2168) is one of kind (disposition versus act) rather than degree, direction, or constitutional level -- confirmed by the grammatical difference between adjective (state of being) and verb (performed action) as noted at Stage 1 (M0.5.2, M0.5.4).

3142.text: Both patterns occur: in Ps.50.23 and Ps.116.17 thanksgiving follows recognition of benefit/salvation already received (a belief precedes the act), while in Josh.7.19 the call to give todah (confession) precedes and is meant to produce a changed belief/admission in Achan -- the offering can express a settled conviction or be the means of producing one.

3166.text: Where a body link exists, it runs from inner disposition/soul outward through the body (bringing an offering, singing, speaking) -- soul/spirit expressing through bodily/material act; there is no evidence of the reverse direction (the body/ritual feeding back to shape the soul) within these occurrences themselves.

3167.text: Todah moves outward from the human person toward God (never onto the person from an external spirit); its sequence runs from an inward recognition of divine benefit to an outward act of speech or offering directed to God -- a soul-to-expression movement, with no instance of external spiritual origination.

3176.text: The origin is consistently single -- the human worshipper (individual or corporate) as the one who offers, sings, or confesses todah toward God -- across every context (legal-cultic, psalmic, prophetic, historical); it does not change to a different originating source in any occurrence.

3193.text: Across this pass's occurrences the surface form 'give thanks' overwhelmingly renders the Hiphil stem in liturgical/doxological contexts (e.g. Ps.138.2, Ps.106.1, Ps.111.1, Ps.44.8, Ps.86.12, Ps.28.7, 1Chr.16.35/8/41, Ps.54.6, Ps.75.1x2, Ps.92.1, Ps.106.47, Ps.122.4, Ps.140.13, 1Chr.16.34, Ps.107.1, Ps.118.1/28/29, Ps.30.4, Ps.97.12, Ps.30.12, Ps.9.1, Ps.79.13, Ps.145.10, Ps.118.19, Ps.57.9, Ps.108.3) -- a large, internally consistent block where the verb names a vocal, addressed act of gratitude toward the Lord's name, character, or acts, with no confession-of-sin sense present in any of these.

3200.text: Across this pass's occurrences the core Hiphil imperative/perfect/participle sense 'give thanks/praise' recurs as the dominant pattern in liturgical contexts: Isa.12.1, 2Chr.30.22, 2Chr.7.6, 2Chr.20.21, 2Chr.31.2, Ezra.3.11, Neh.12.24, Ps.109.30, Isa.12.4, Jer.33.11, Ps.7.17, 1Chr.16.4, 1Chr.29.13, Ps.35.18, Ps.118.21, Ps.52.9, Ps.107.8/15/21/31, Ps.100.4, Ps.136.1/2/3/26, Ps.33.2, 2Chr.5.13, 1Chr.16.7, Neh.12.46, Ps.138.4, Ps.138.1, 2Chr.7.3, 1Chr.23.30, 1Chr.25.3, Ps.142.7, Neh.11.17 -- all render the same basic act of vocal, often corporate/musical, thanksgiving directed at the Lord, frequently anchored by the refrain 'his steadfast love endures forever.'

3215.text: Yes, the mechanism differs across contexts: in the cultic/temple context it operates through appointed liturgical office and musical instrumentation (1Chr.16.4, 2Chr.5.13, 1Chr.25.3 -- Levites appointed, with lyre/trumpets); in the personal-devotional context it operates through spontaneous individual speech-vow (Ps.9.1, Ps.86.12 'with my whole heart'); in the penitential context it operates through a required ritual or intercessory-prayer act (Lev.16.21's scapegoat confession, Dan.9.4's extended prayer of confession) -- three distinct mechanisms (institutional/musical, personal/vocal, ritual/legal) all realizing the same root verb.

3227.text: The characteristic operates differently within existing covenantal bonds versus across relational distance: within Israel's covenant relationship it is richly institutionalized (temple liturgy, appointed Levites, e.g. 1Chr.16.4) while directed toward 'the nations'/'peoples' it functions as missionary declaration or eschatological hope (2Sam.22.50 'I will praise you... among the nations'; Ps.67.3/5 'let all the peoples praise you') -- the covenant people's own liturgical practice differs in mode from the hoped-for extension to outsiders.

3241.text: Where a human party leads others into the characteristic (David appointing Levites to give thanks, 1Chr.16.4; Hezekiah speaking encouragingly before the people give thanks, 2Chr.30.22), the giver's own inner condition is one of prior established devotion and administrative/pastoral care -- appointing and encouraging others toward thanksgiving presupposes the giver's own settled orientation toward God's worship.

3261.text: The nearest adjacent characteristic is praise/halal (H1984B, 'to praise, boast'), frequently paired directly with yadah as a near-synonym (e.g. 1Chr.16.4, Ps.100.4). What distinguishes them: yadah carries the root sense of casting-forth acknowledgment (often content-specific, naming a reason -- 'for he is good') and covers confession of sin as well, whereas halal centers on exaltation/boasting in another's worth and lacks the confession-of-sin branch.

3399.text: In Ps.10.13 darash surfaces as 'call to account' rather than 'seek/inquire' -- this is a specialized forensic-requiring sense (cf. sense 1a6 'to investigate, enquire', extended toward legal reckoning) distinct from the devotional 'seek' sense used in Ps.10.4 just verses earlier in the same psalm, showing the root's range from religious pursuit to judicial demand within a single context.

3403.text: In Ps.10.13, other M-codes present (M58 wicked, M30 renounce, M47 heart) describe the wicked's rejection of God, while darash's own forensic sense ('call to account') stands as the rhetorical question's target, not modified by those terms directly.

3410.text: In Ps.10.13, the 'call to account' operation is rhetorically denied by the wicked (party) regarding God's (party) prerogative to require reckoning of him.

3476.text: In Esth.2.21, 1Sam.24.9, Num.35.23, and 1Kgs.20.7 the surface sense shifts from the base gloss 'seek/desire' toward a conspiratorial/hostile sense 'to plot against, seek to harm/kill' -- a marked negative-valence divergence from the neutral-to-positive base gloss. By contrast in 2Chr.15.4 the surface sense aligns with the base devotional gloss (seeking God). This shows the same lexeme's stepGloss splits sharply by direction of the object across these occurrences.

3480.text: 1Kgs.20.7: the operation word 'sent' (H7971G, role-T3) is initiated by Ben-hadad (implied 'he') and directed 'to me' (the king of Israel), demanding wives, children, silver and gold; this sending is the concrete operation behind the accusation that he is 'seeking trouble' (H1245).

3486.text: In 1Sam.24.9 and 1Kgs.20.7 the only other M-code present is M58/M24 ('harm'/'trouble', the object sought); H1245 names the act of pursuit whose object is itself named by the M24/M58 term -- the two are tightly bound as verb-and-object within the same accusation.

4022.text: In Acts 15:17 (quoting Amos 9:12 LXX) ekzeteo carries the nuance of the Gentiles' eschatological, corporate turning to seek the Lord — a diligent/earnest theological seeking rather than casual search, its impact here universalizing the seek-motif beyond Israel; this contrasts with other occurrences where ekzeteo denotes legal demand (Luke 11:50f) or personal supplication (Heb 12:17).

4023.text: Other M-code tags present in this verse (M72, M42) belong to other clusters (Lord-title, calling/naming) and are not directly related to the seeking-action from this cluster's vantage point; ekzeteo names the approach toward the Lord while the M42/M72 words name the Lord's own identity and calling of the Gentiles — parallel but distinct functions.

4024.text: The operation 'seek' is initiated by the remnant of mankind and all the Gentiles (party-tagged group), directed toward 'the Lord' as the sought object — establishing a movement from the human party toward the divine party.

4122.text: In Song 5.6, 1Chr 16.10, Ps 105.3, and Isa 45.19 the surface gloss 'sought/seek/Seek' sits squarely within the base sense of active searching/desiring with no notable divergence.

4123.text: No other M-code characteristic is tagged in Song.5.6 alongside H1245's seeking.

4128.text: In Song.5.6, H1245 (sought) is an operation initiated by the female speaker ('I sought him'), directed toward her absent beloved -- a party present by reference though physically gone; the operation fails ('found him not').

4309.text: No other M-code characteristic is present in John.5.18; the Jews' seeking-to-kill is the sole characteristic-bearing term in this verse within the cluster registry.

4319.text: In John.5.18 the seeking-to-kill operation is initiated by 'the Jews' (party T11) and directed toward Jesus (party, implied by 'him'), driven by his Sabbath-breaking and equality-with-God claims.

4334.text: John.5.18 'seeking...to kill him' uses the same lethal-intent idiom as the OT 'seek the life' construction (noted explicitly in the meaning tree as inherited from Hebrew) -- a marked intensification beyond the neutral base gloss of 'look for', carrying deliberate hostile intent; this matches the Jer.21.7/46.26 pattern rather than John's other, more neutral uses of zeteo (e.g. seeking Jesus to hear him).

4468.text: In Jer.30.17 H1875 surfaces as 'cares' (participle, 'no one cares for her') rather than the more common 'seek/inquire' gloss - here the nuance shifts fully to the compassionate-tending sense (1a8, 'to seek with care, care for'), impacting the verse's meaning as an accusation of total abandonment/neglect of Zion, contrasting with the cultic-inquiry sense dominant in Jer.10.21 and 1Chr.15.13.

4472.text: In Jer.30.17 no other M-code characteristic co-occurs with H1875 in this verse's role tags.

4477.text: In Jer.30.17 the caring-operation (H1875, 'cares') is negated - no one initiates care toward Zion, the party in view - marking an absent party-to-party operation of compassionate tending.

4770.text: In Acts.9.11 'look for' (imperative, seeking a specific named man) sits squarely within the base gloss of physical searching for a person; no divergent nuance from the general stepGloss.

4772.text: In Acts.16.10 'sought' (aorist, 'we sought to go on into Macedonia') carries the ordinary sense of striving/endeavoring to act; falls within base gloss with no notable shift.

4876.text: In 1Sam.9.9 H1875 (inquire of God) co-occurs with M43 (prophet) and M02/M50 (face-idiom terms) -- the inquiry act is the means by which the prophet's revelatory role is accessed; this is the first pass over this verse.

4897.text: 1Sam.9.9 uses H1875 in its specifically cultic sense of consulting God via a seer -- the narrator's parenthetical note on seer/prophet terminology highlights this as the technical religious-inquiry sense, sharper than a generic 'ask' gloss.

4900.text: In 1Sam.9.9 the inquiry is initiated by 'a man' (a generic Israelite party), directed toward God via the seer -- a human party consulting the divine party through an intermediary.

4934.text: In 2Sam.21.2 (Saul's zeal to strike down the Gibeonites), the surface sense 'sought [to strike down]' sits within the base gloss of intent/desire (1a4) with no notable divergence.

4952.text: In 2Sam.21.2, Saul (party, T8) is the initiator of the seeking-operation, directed toward striking down the Gibeonites (T11 party) -- the seeking is hostile/lethal in intent, aimed at a specific ethnic group.

4962.text: In 2Sam.21.2, M83 (sought) co-occurs with M03 (remnant/H3499A) and M18 (zeal/H7065), but the seeking-operation itself targets the Gibeonites' destruction and is not functionally tied to the remnant-status or zeal terms beyond sharing the verse; no prior relational context exists for this verse.

4987.text: In Neh.5.12 'require nothing' shifts H1245 toward a specific legal/financial sense of exacting repayment or interest, narrower than the general 'seek' gloss -- the impact here is a promise of restraint from demanding restitution, a nuance of formal renunciation of claim compared to the more common 'seek/inquire' occurrences.

4991.text: In Neh.5.12 the speakers (nobles/officials) direct the operation of NOT requiring repayment toward the debtors, a self-restraining pledge announced before the priests.

4995.text: No other M-code characteristic co-occurs with H1245 in Neh.5.12 (aside from M11/M81 on 'restore', which is a different characteristic not co-analyzed here as home); from H1245's own vantage, this pledge of non-exaction stands independent of restitution's own semantic thread.

5037.text: In Neh.5.12 'promised' is a contextual rendering of the general 'word/matter' gloss, narrowing it specifically to a sworn oath-commitment; the impact is that the abstract word-sense is pressed into legal/covenantal service as a binding promise before priestly witnesses.

5059.text: No other M-code characteristic co-occurs in this verse alongside the seeking of the priesthood.

5068.text: God is the initiator here ('by those who did not seek me' being sought BY God), an inversion where God is subject seeking out a nation that itself did not seek him -- the direction is God toward the unresponsive nation.

5088.text: M42 (called, H7121H) co-occurs describing the nation not being 'called by God's name'; it characterizes the unresponsive nation's identity, distinct from the inquiring/seeking dynamic itself which here is enacted by God, not the nation.

5166.text: In Prov.1.28 'seek me diligently' uses H7836 in its ordinary earnest-seeking sense (personified Wisdom as object); this sits squarely within the base gloss, though the futility (seeking too late, after refusing to listen earlier) is supplied by narrative context, not the verb's own shift.

5167.text: The seeking operation is initiated by 'they' (those who earlier refused wisdom's call) and directed toward personified Wisdom ('me'), paired with 'call upon me' and answered by refusal ('I will not answer') -- an operation of belated, futile pursuit.

5168.text: M42 (call) and M22 (answer) are also present, describing the paired invocation and refusal; H7836's diligent seeking supplies the futile intensified pursuit that follows the call, but the M-codes describe distinct acts (calling vs seeking) rather than one shaping the other's meaning.

5234.text: In Exod.33.7 'sought' describes habitual cultic practice (everyone who sought the LORD would go to the tent of meeting) -- a straightforward instance of the base gloss with no unusual nuance.

5235.text: In Lam.1.19 'sought' takes food as its object rather than God or a person -- a literal survival-seeking sense; the impact here is pathos (priests/elders seeking mere sustenance while starving), a physical-need nuance distinct from the cultic/relational seeking seen in Exod.33.7 and 2Chr.7.14.

5236.text: In 2Chr.7.14 'seek my face' is the classic idiomatic combination (seek + face) meaning seeking God's favor/presence in penitence -- squarely within the base gloss's known idiomatic use, no further divergence.

5239.text: No other M-code characteristic is present in Exod.33.7 among home-cluster terms; seeking the LORD here stands as the verse's sole relational-characteristic focus, establishing the tent-of-meeting practice.

5240.text: M-code terms present in Lam.1.19 (M51 lovers, M14 deceived, M36 priests, M11/M81 revive) surround seeking but are not directly tied to it relationally: the lovers' deception and the priests' death are the CAUSE of the desperate seeking, not a characteristic seeking itself relates to -- seeking's own contribution is marking the community's reduced state, food-seeking as last resort after betrayal and death.

5241.text: In 2Chr.7.14, seeking (H1245, seek my face) sits within a tightly-related chain with M09 (humble themselves) and M60 (forgive): seeking is the middle act -- following humbling and preceding turning -- that directs the humbled disposition specifically toward God's face/presence, making it the pivot that connects self-abasement to the divine forgiving response.

5242.text: In Exod.33.7, H1245 is the role-T3 operation: 'everyone' (the party) initiates the seeking, directed toward 'the LORD' (party), the action performed by going out to the tent of meeting.

5243.text: In 2Chr.7.14, H1245 is the role-T3 operation: 'my people' (party) initiate the seeking, directed toward God's 'face' (representing the divine party) as part of the penitential sequence.

5244.text: In Lam.1.19, H1245 is role-T3: the speaker's priests and elders (party) initiate the seeking, directed toward 'food' (an object, not a party) to revive their strength -- so the operation is party-to-object rather than party-to-party.

5259.text: In Isa.55.6 'Seek the LORD' is the paradigm sincere imperative use of darash, squarely within the base gloss of urgent covenantal seeking; no divergent nuance.

5260.text: In Isa.62.12 'Sought Out' functions as a passive-participle EPITHET/name for the restored city rather than describing an act of seeking performed by the city -- a nominalized, identity-conferring nuance distinct from the active-seeking sense elsewhere; the impact is to make the city's new identity itself the proof that it is desired/valued rather than forsaken.

5264.text: No other M-code characteristic is present in Isa.55.6 among the tagged roles; seeking the LORD stands as the verse's sole relational-characteristic focus, paired only with the imperative to call on him.

5265.text: In Isa.62.12, H1875 ('Sought Out') is tightly related to M61 (Holy) and M79 (Redeemed): together they form a triad of covenant-identity epithets for the restored city -- holy status, redeemed status, and sought-out status jointly constitute the new name replacing the old reproach; being 'sought out' specifically supplies the relational proof that the city is now wanted rather than abandoned.

7056.text: G1567 (ekzeteo) and G1934 (epizeteo) both intensify the base zeteo root via a directional prefix (ek- 'out/thoroughly' vs epi- 'upon/toward'), and both share the same semantic split visible cross-strong: a devotional/diligent-seeking sense (ekzeteo: Acts.15.17, Heb.11.6, Rom.3.11, 1Pet.1.10; epizeteo: Heb.11.14, Heb.13.14, Acts.13.7) alongside a demanding/legal-exaction sense (ekzeteo: Luke.11.50-51, blood 'required'; epizeteo: Matt.12.39, Matt.16.4, Mark.8.12, Luke.11.29, demanding a sign; Acts.19.39, formal legal matter). Both Greek terms thus independently develop the same two-pole range (earnest seeking <-> exacting demand) from the same simple root, making them the closest pair in this subgroup.

7059.text: Cross-strong, the two Greek members (ekzeteo, epizeteo) both attest a passive/legal-exaction voice pattern absent from shachar entirely: ekzeteo's future/aorist passive 'will be required/may be charged' (Luke.11.50-51) and epizeteo's passive-adjacent 'is matter of question/demand' senses in LSJ have no shachar counterpart -- shachar occurs only in Qal/Piel active-voice forms across all 12 occurrences, meaning the Hebrew member of this subgroup carries no attested passive 'held-to-account' construction, unlike its two Greek subgroup-mates.

7060.text: Within the subgroup's shared 'intensification of the base seek-root' logic, ekzeteo's intensifying element (ek-, 'out/thoroughly') most naturally supports a completion/exhaustiveness reading (searching OUT fully, exacting an account IN FULL -- e.g. 'from the foundation of the world,' Luke.11.50), whereas epizeteo's intensifying element (epi-, 'upon/toward/further') most naturally supports a directedness/insistence reading (pressing TOWARD an object, seeking FURTHER/again -- LSJ's 'seek for besides,' 'inquire further'). Both belong to this subgroup's 'thoroughness or added directedness' core description, but each realizes a different half of it: ekzeteo leans toward thoroughness, epizeteo toward directedness/insistence.

7068.text: Within this single surface-form batch ('cares', 'seek', 'sought'), H1875 spans a very wide register: the overwhelming majority of 'seek'/'sought' occurrences name devotional/cultic pursuit of the Lord (Ps.77.2, 2Chr.20.3, 1Chr.22.19, Hos.10.12, 2Chr.14.7, 2Chr.26.5) or of false gods (2Chr.25.15, 2Chr.25.20, 2Chr.17.3 negated), while two occurrences ('cares', Ps.142.4 and Jer.30.17) shift entirely to an interpersonal-compassion sense ('no one cares for my soul' / 'for whom no one cares') with no cultic or consultative content at all -- the same root covers both vertical (human-to-God) and horizontal (person-to-person) relational concern.

7073.text: Across this pass's 'inquire' surface-form cluster (1Kgs.22.8, 2Chr.18.7, 2Kgs.22.13/2Chr.34.21, 2Kgs.3.11, 2Kgs.1.2/1.3/1.6/1.16, 2Kgs.8.8, 1Kgs.14.5, Ezek.20.3, 1Sam.28.7, Jer.10.21, Gen.25.22, Exod.18.15, Deut.12.30, 1Sam.9.9, 1Kgs.22.7/2Chr.18.6, 2Kgs.22.18/2Chr.34.26, Isa.8.19, Jer.37.7, 2Chr.32.31, Isa.19.3, Zeph.1.6, Isa.11.10, Ezek.20.1, 1Chr.21.30, Isa.9.13) the term consistently denotes formal consultation of a deity or authoritative source (the Lord, a prophet, an oracle, Baal-zebub, mediums/necromancers) for a verdict or answer -- the single largest and most cohesive sense-cluster in H1875's full occurrence set, matching this subgroup's core description of institutional/cultic resort to authority for guidance.

7074.text: The 'Seek' surface form in this pass (Amos.5.4/5.6/5.14, 1Chr.16.11, Ps.105.4, Isa.55.6, Isa.34.16) is used almost exclusively in imperative form as an urgent devotional/covenantal exhortation ('Seek the LORD/his strength/good and live') rather than as narrative report of consultation -- a distinct sub-mode of this subgroup's formal-inquiry sense: exhortation to habitual, life-orienting seeking of God rather than a single act of consulting an oracle for a specific verdict.

7093.text: Ps.10.13 and Ps.10.15 both render darash as legal-accountability terms ('call to account'/'account') within the same psalm, applying the forensic-demand sense of darash to God's judicial reckoning with the wicked -- consistent with the Gen.9.5/Gen.42.22 'reckoning' pattern but here directed at moral wickedness rather than bloodshed specifically.

7099.text: Isa.62.12's 'Sought Out' functions as a passive-participle EPITHET/name for the restored city rather than describing an active act of seeking performed by anyone in the verse -- a nominalized, identity-conferring nuance unique among this pass's occurrences, making darash itself the substance of a proper name/title.

7167.text: The subgroup shows clear future-fullness orientation: Heb.11.14 and Heb.13.14 (epizeteo) name a 'homeland' and 'city that is to come' not yet possessed; Acts.15.17 (ekzeteo) envisions Gentiles yet to seek the Lord eschatologically; Isa.26.9 (shachar) links earnest seeking to a future state when 'the inhabitants of the world learn righteousness.' The movement is consistently toward something the person does not yet have -- a not-yet-attained relational or covenantal completeness.

7180.text: The characteristic is blocked or fruitless under conditions of unbelief (Rom.3.11, 'no one seeks for God' as part of a universal indictment of sinfulness), of prior settled disqualification (Heb.12.17, Esau finds 'no chance to repent' though he sought with tears), of hostile testing rather than genuine inquiry (Matt.12.39/16.4, an 'evil and adulterous generation' demands a sign), and of persistent unresponsiveness to prior calls (Prov.1.28, wisdom's earlier call refused, so later diligent seeking finds no answer). No adversarial-spirit interference is shown in any occurrence; blockage arises from the seeker's own unbelief, prior refusal, or a closed opportunity, not from another spirit's distortion.

7182.text: Yes. Within existing covenantal bonds (Israel and God), seeking operates as restorative return after distress (Hos.5.15, Ps.78.34) -- an insider's turning back. Across relational distance/difference (Gentiles, outsiders), seeking operates as a fresh, boundary-crossing inclusion: Acts.15.17 explicitly extends ekzeteo to 'the remnant of mankind... and all the Gentiles who are called by my name,' widening the covenantal seeking beyond Israel's existing bond.

7183.text: The characteristic crosses covenantal boundaries: while most OT (shachar) occurrences operate within Israel's covenant relationship with YHWH, Acts.15.17 (ekzeteo, quoting Amos 9:12 LXX) explicitly extends the seeking-of-the-Lord motif to Gentiles 'who are called by my name,' showing the characteristic is not confined to covenant insiders but is projected forward to include outsiders under a widened covenantal frame.

7207.text: The characteristic excludes/resists casual or half-hearted inquiry at its edge -- its intensifying prefixes/root explicitly mark it off from a merely passing glance or occasional interest (zeteo's plain form); it also resists premature closure, refusing to settle for partial or token search (Prov.1.28's failed 'diligent' seeking shows the characteristic still names genuine effort even when unsuccessful, distinguishing it from giving up).

7212.text: The sequence is developmental and causal rather than merely correlational: acknowledgment of guilt causally opens the way for seeking (Hos.5.15's 'until'), and seeking causally produces finding (Prov.8.17's promise), showing a real chain of cause-and-effect rather than accidental co-occurrence -- though the chain can be broken (Prov.1.28's failed seeking shows the causal chain is conditioned on timing/prior response, not automatic).

7218.text: The distinction from the nearest neighbor (plain zeteo) is one of degree, not kind -- the subgroup's members intensify the same basic act of seeking rather than naming a categorically different action; within the subgroup itself, ekzeteo and epizeteo differ from each other by direction (ek- 'out/thoroughly' vs epi- 'upon/toward,' per prior char_reading observations), while shachar differs from both by constitutional mechanism (an inherent root-level intensifier rather than a compounded directional prefix).

7274.text: In Isa.65.1 God's readiness to be sought by those who did not ask reveals his own disposition/perception that he is available and near even to those not yet oriented toward him -- a divine self-disclosure of gracious accessibility rather than a human perception.

7281.text: The capacity to inquire/seek belongs to created design -- humanity's original capacity for relationship and dependence on God through consultation (Exod.18.15, Gen.25.22, 1Sam.9.9) -- but its exercise is repeatedly corrupted by the fallen condition, redirected toward false gods, mediums, and necromancers (1Sam.28.7, Deut.18.11, 2Kgs.1.2, Isa.19.3), showing the characteristic itself spans both created design and fallen misdirection depending on its object.

7296.text: The human-to-God direction of seeking reveals a relationship of dependence and covenantal trust: the seeker approaches God as the source of guidance, deliverance, and life (Ps.34.4 'I sought the Lord, and he answered me and delivered me'; Amos.5.4 'Seek me and live'), showing the relationship is characterized by the human party's reliance on God's willingness to respond and God's reciprocal availability to be found (Isa.55.6 'while he may be found').

7303.text: God's extension of the characteristic (his willingness to be sought/found) is shown as both conditional and responsive: conditional on genuine seeking ('If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever', 1Chr.28.9), yet also shown as gracious and unconditioned in Isa.65.1 ('I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me') -- God's self-disclosure as available to be inquired of exceeds strict conditionality, showing both a covenantal-conditional pattern and a gracious-responsive pattern.

7304.text: God's extension of the characteristic -- his readiness to be sought even by those who did not ask (Isa.65.1) and his invitation 'Seek me and live' (Amos.5.4) -- shows a disposition of gracious accessibility and desire for relationship with humanity, contrasted with his refusal to be inquired of by the unrepentant and idolatrous (Ezek.20.3, 20.31), revealing a disposition that is both inviting and holy/discerning.

7319.text: Seeking consistently PRECEDES finding/being found and its resulting blessings: Jer.29.13 'You will seek me and find me'; Isa.55.6 'Seek the Lord while he may be found'; 1Chr.28.9 'If you seek him, he will be found by you' -- the sequence is invariably seek-then-find, never the reverse, establishing seeking as the necessary antecedent condition.

12479.text: A person chooses a thing or place for oneself by sight or use: "the sons of God saw that the daughters of man were attractive. And they took as their wives any they chose" (Gen 6:2); "Lot chose for himself all the Jordan Valley" (Gen 13:11), and they separated; David chose five smooth stones (1Sa 17:40); the bulls of the contest on Carmel are chosen (1Ki 18:23, 25).

12481.text: God chooses a person for a task or office: priests and Levites, the king, David, Solomon, the servant, witnesses. Choosing goes with bringing near: "The one whom he chooses he will bring near to him" (Num 16:5); "Blessed is the one you choose and bring near" (Psa 65:4). The choice is shown, not argued: "the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout" (Num 17:5). It is followed by a charge: "the Lord has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary; be strong and do it" (1Ch 28:10). In the servant it is joined to God's soul and Spirit: "my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him" (Isa 42:1; Mat 12:18).

12482.text: God chooses a people, and the verses give love as the ground and deny number: "It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the Lord set his love on you and chose you" (Deu 7:7); "the Lord set his heart in love on your fathers and chose their offspring" (Deu 10:15). The choosing makes them "a people for his treasured possession" (Deu 7:6) and "his chosen ones" (Psa 105:6). It is joined to not casting off, "I have chosen you and not cast you off" (Isa 41:9), and to a purpose: "that you may know and believe me" (Isa 43:10).

12487.text: Inner-being words stand beside choosing: God's heart in what he chooses, "My eyes and my heart will be there for all time" (2Ch 7:16); his soul in his chosen servant, "my chosen, in whom my soul delights" (Isa 42:1; Mat 12:18); the people's heart and soul turned toward the chosen city in repentance (1Ki 8:48; 2Ch 6:38); the soul's delight in chosen ways (Isa 66:3); the soul choosing death (Job 7:15); the heart given a worth (Pro 10:20); the soul's appetite, "whenever you desire" (Deu 12:21; Deu 18:6); the self humbled in a fast God does not choose (Isa 58:5); "one deeply despised" whom the Lord has chosen (Isa 49:7).

12492.text: God chooses what he wants: "Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness" (Isa 58:6), set against a fast of bowing the head (Isa 58:5); "To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the Lord than sacrifice" (Pro 21:3); "I will appoint over her whomever I choose. For who is like me?" (Jer 49:19; Jer 50:44).

12493.text: A person chooses against God: other gods, "the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you" (Judg 10:14); their own ways, "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations" (Isa 66:3); what God does not delight in (Isa 65:12). The verses name what drives or follows such choosing: "your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty" (Job 15:5); "Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways" (Pro 3:31); "this you have chosen rather than affliction" (Job 36:21). Shame follows: "you shall blush for the gardens that you have chosen" (Isa 1:29); "an abomination is he who chooses you" (Isa 41:24).

12510.text: The plan to harm is named and checked: "Whoever plans to do evil will be called a schemer" (Pro 24:8); "if you have been devising evil, put your hand on your mouth" (Pro 30:32); of the false witness, "you shall do to him as he had meant to do to his brother" (Deu 19:19).

12518.text: Looking ahead weighs before it acts: a king "will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand" (Luk 14:31); "She considers a field and buys it" (Pro 31:16); "consider it, take counsel, and speak" (Judg 19:30). It plans without knowing: "on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix" (Act 27:12), "supposing that they had obtained their purpose" (Act 27:13), "they planned if possible to run the ship ashore" (Act 27:39). A plan carries a word: "Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say Yes, yes and No, no at the same time?" (2Co 1:17). Plans part people: "Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark" (Act 15:37); Joseph of Arimathea "had not consented to their decision and action" (Luk 23:51). And a plan can be for another's good: "because an excellent spirit was in him. And the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom" (Dan 6:3).

12522.text: "he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God" (Rom 8:27); "for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose" (Rom 8:28). And a person can refuse it: "the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves" (Luk 7:30).

12524.text: His purpose is before the ages and not from works: "because of his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began" (2Ti 1:9); "in order that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls" (Rom 9:11); "according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will" (Eph 1:11); "the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ" (Eph 1:9); "the eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Eph 3:11); "whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood" (Rom 3:25).
