13122.text: Sequence in Luk 15:25–32: music heard → the servant explains → angry, refuses to go in → the father comes out and entreats → the ledger ("these many years") → "this son of yours" → "this your brother" → (no answer).

13129.text: Sequence in Jos 7; 22:10–34: one man takes → anger on all → defeat → offender removed → anger turns → the memory drives a later confrontation → answer "He knows".

13141.text: Sequence in Isa 57:14–18: God dwells with the contrite spirit → "nor will I always be angry; for the spirit would grow faint before me" → struck, hid face → backsliding "in the way of his own heart" → "I will heal him".

13142.text: Sequence in Isa 63:1–64:12: no one to help → God's arm alone → "I will recount the steadfast love" → "you were angry, and we sinned" → no one who calls → "we are the clay … please look".

13143.text: Sequence in Jer 7:16–29: intercession forbidden → whole families provoke → "Is it I whom they provoke? … themselves" → wrath poured → "did not accept discipline" → "cut off your hair … lament".

13147.text: Sequence in Eze 9:1–10: abominations → mark on those who sigh and groan → slaughter begins at the sanctuary → the prophet alone, face down: "Will you destroy all the remnant?" → "my eye will not spare".

13148.text: Sequence in Eze 16: not satisfied → whoring to provoke → lovers gathered against her → wrath and jealousy → "I will be calm and will no more be angry" → remember and be confounded, "when I atone for you".

13151.text: Sequence in Joe 2:11–14; Jon 3:5–10: the day, "who can endure it?" → return with the heart, fasting, sackcloth → the creed (Joel) or the preached word (Nineveh) → "Who knows?" → (Jonah) God relented.

13169.text: Anger and Fear (M01): Moses afraid of the anger, and heard; afraid, then enraged; angry, then afraid; "do not fear" at another's fierce anger; "not being afraid of the anger of the king"; indignation and fear in one verse.

13197.text: What sets a person's anger off: demand → anger → "Am I in the place of God" (Gen 30:1–2); no regard → very angry → face fell (Gen 4:5); saw no homage → filled with fury → sought to destroy all the Jews (Est 3:5–6); "I thought" → rage (2Ki 5:11–12); afraid → withdraw → enraged (Dan 11:30); heard → filled with wrath → drove him out (Luk 4:28–29); passions at war within → quarrels (Jam 4:1).

13202.text: What a person's anger leads to: heard → anger → broke the tablets (Exo 32:19); angry → put them in custody (Gen 40:2–3); company of the angry → learning his ways → a snare (Pro 22:24–25); fret → tends only to evil (Psa 37:8); angry → afraid (2Sa 6:8–9); angry → cried to the Lord all night (1Sa 15:11); Naboth's word → vexed and sullen → would eat no food (1Ki 21:4); provoke your children → lest they become discouraged (Col 3:21).

13205.text: Anger answered in kind: no god, idols → provoked → "I will … provoke them" (Deu 32:21); pours wrath on neighbours → the Lord's cup comes around to you (Hab 2:15–16); they would not hear → I would not hear (Zec 7:13).

13217.text: Same root, no anger: zāʿap̄ as a downcast face, sāʿar as a troubled mind, ʿāšan as Sinai's smoke, ʿebrāh as pride, zestos as the heat of works.

13221.text: Hope inside the lament, and the anger said to end: "therefore I have hope" (Lam 3:21); "he does not afflict from his heart" (Lam 3:33); "he touched me and made me stand up" (Dan 8:18); the wise refined (Dan 11:35).

13230.text: U1 §37, Gen 27:41–45: the reading says murder planned in his heart; the ESV says "Esau said to himself" (Gen 27:41); the text carries H3820A lēḇ, rendered "himself", tagged M47.

13241.text: Where the angry person's own heart or spirit is named: in the narratives it is rare (2Ki 6:11; Est 5:9; Act 7:54; Act 17:16; Eze 3:14), and in the wisdom books frequent (Job 36:13; Pro 6:14; 14:29; 16:32; 19:3; Ecc 2:23; 7:3; 7:9; 11:10); the narratives show anger by what is done.

13255.text: Face L. Acting to turn it away: Hits / verses: 18 / 16; Who speaks or acts: Moses and the judges, Joshua, Rehoboam, Oded and the chiefs of Ephraim, Hezekiah, Ezra's officials, Jeremiah, the king of Nineveh, the humble; Example verses: Num 25:4; Jos 7:26; 2Ch 12:12; 2Ch 29:10; Jon 3:9; Zep 2:3.

13257.text: Face P. At a demand or a will thwarted: Hits / verses: 5 / 4; Who is angry, and at whom: Jacob at Rachel; Balaam at the donkey; Balak at Balaam; Ephraim's army at Judah; Example verses: Gen 30:2; Num 22:27; Num 24:10; 2Ch 25:10.

13283.text: one man took the devoted things → the people broke faith → anger (Jos 7:1); dealt with → anger turned (Jos 7:26).

13322.text: The heat family outside the anger tag (ḥāmam, OT-15): "All of them are hot as an oven" (Hos 7:7).

13337.text: Face 2M. Called down on others: Hits / verses: 3 / 3; Who speaks or acts: David, Asaph, Jeremiah; Example verses: Psa 59:13; Psa 79:6; Jer 10:25.

13356.text: What precedes it (new for this word): news and alarm; a thing seen; an expectation thwarted; a refusal; blood left uncovered; a written book heard: Verses: Dan 11:44; Est 5:9; 2Ki 5:11; Est 1:12; Eze 24:8; 2Ki 22:13.

13390.text: devoured Jacob → "Pour out your wrath on the nations" (Jer 10:25); consumed → "that they may know that God rules" (Psa 59:13).

13398.text: saw no homage → filled with fury → sought to destroy all the Jews (Est 3:5–6); glad of heart → saw → filled with wrath (Est 5:9); "I thought" → rage (2Ki 5:11–12).

13411.text: Face 3D. Turned, withdrawn, not executed; or not turned back: Hits / verses: 7 / 6; Toward: his people, Ephraim, Judah; Other parties named: the reason stated: "I am God and not a man"; Manasseh's provocations; Example verses: Hos 11:9; Psa 85:3; Jos 7:26; 2Ki 23:26; Jer 30:24.

13427.text: Face 3T. Angry at what God does: Hits / verses: 4 / 4; Who, and at whom: David, Samuel, Jonah; Example verses: 2Sa 6:8; 1Ch 13:11; 1Sa 15:11; Jon 4:1.

13441.text: Its form (new): a burning that is kindled, increases, is turned or not turned; a weight heavier than sand; a lodger in the heart: Verses: Num 32:14; Jos 7:26; Pro 27:3; Job 6:2–3; Ecc 7:9 (AG-103, 110, 142, 145).

13443.text: What precedes it (unit 1, extended): no regard; another's honour; a work going forward; a charge; a rebuke; a wrong done to another; God's act; God's word: Verses: Gen 4:5; 1Sa 18:8; Neh 4:7; 2Sa 3:8; 2Ch 16:10; Neh 5:6; 2Sa 6:8; 1Sa 15:11.

13447.text: What it answers to (unit 2, extended): God's anger as the answer to a cry, sung by the one delivered: Verses: 2Sa 22:7–8; Exo 15:7 (AG-108).

13453.text: F.8: What emerged: God's anger as the answer to a cry, sung by the one delivered (2Sa 22:7–8; Exo 15:7; Hab 3:8, AG-108).; What it changes elsewhere: Extends AG-20; the parties around God's anger include the one it rescues (ruling 6.2).; Where: 10.13; 10.9.

13460.text: called in distress → heard → earth reeled, because he was angry (2Sa 22:7–8; Psa 18:6–7).

13461.text: heart to make a covenant → fierce anger turn away (2Ch 29:10); yield → turn away (2Ch 30:8); turned from their evil way → God relented (Jon 3:10); heap of stones → turned from his burning anger (Jos 7:26).

13482.text: angry → afraid → "How can the ark … come to me?" (2Sa 6:8–9); angry → cried to the Lord all night (1Sa 15:11).

13494.text: 2Ki 6:11 says "greatly troubled": there is no anger word in the verse.

13508.text: Face 4I. On the nations and enemies; the earth before it: Hits / verses: 18 / 15; Toward: Egypt, Assyria, Ammon, Babylon, Edom, Gog, his enemies; Other parties named: heavens, earth, rivers, sea, rocks; destroying angels; his servants; Example verses: Jer 10:10; Nah 1:6; Isa 30:27; Psa 7:11; Isa 66:14; Mal 1:4.

13514.text: Face 4O. Meribah: Hits / verses: 11 / 9; Who: the people quarrel; God is angered; Moses and Aaron are barred; Levi was tested there; Example verses: Exo 17:7; Num 20:13, 24; Psa 95:8; Psa 81:7; Psa 106:32.

13517.text: Face 4R. At a rebuke, a refusal or an unexpected answer; vexed and sullen: Hits / verses: 6 / 5; Who, and at whom: Naaman, Uzziah, Asa, Ahab; Example verses: 2Ki 5:11; 2Ch 26:19; 1Ki 21:4; 1Ki 20:43.

13528.text: Face 4AB. Troubled, downcast or storm-tossed: Hits / verses: 5 / 5; What: prisoners' faces, a eunuch's fear, a king distressed for Daniel, a king's mind, Zion; Example verses: Gen 40:6; Dan 1:10; Dan 6:14; 2Ki 6:11; Isa 54:11.

13535.text: One root, different things (new): ʿebrāh: wrath and pride (AG-188); zāʿam: anger and the spoken curse (AG-179); zāʿap̄: rage, a downcast face, a sullen king, the sea (AG-184, 195, 197); sāʿar: a storm and a troubled mind (AG-195); ʿāšan: Sinai's smoke and God's anger (AG-176): Verses: Pro 21:24; Num 23:8; Gen 40:6; 1Ki 21:4; 2Ki 6:11; Exo 19:18; Psa 74:1.

13537.text: What precedes it (units 1 and 3, extended): a word heard (AG-149); a refusal; an instruction unexpected; a rebuke (AG-184); an order not kept (AG-183); suspicion (AG-185); fear (Dan 11:30); hunger (Isa 8:21); one's own folly (Pro 19:3): Verses: Psa 78:21; Est 1:12; 2Ki 5:11; 2Ch 26:19; Exo 16:20; 1Sa 29:4; Dan 11:30; Isa 8:21; Pro 19:3.

13547.text: F.9: What emerged: Same root, no anger: zāʿap̄ as a downcast face; sāʿar as a troubled mind; ʿāšan as Sinai's smoke; ʿebrāh as pride (AG-176, 188, 195).; What it changes elsewhere: RS: Ch 11 §4 Storm calls 2Ki 6:11 the angry king's mind; the verse says "greatly troubled". To be corrected when Ch 11 is next touched; listed for the overview appendix (#1947).; Where: 11 §4.

13551.text: hearts diamond-hard, lest they hear → great anger came (Zec 7:12); they would not hear → I would not hear (7:13); blesses himself in his heart → anger will smoke against that man (Deu 29:19–20).

13570.text: does not repent → God will whet his sword (Psa 7:12); indignation against enemies → your heart shall rejoice (Isa 66:14); angry forever with Edom → "Great is the Lord" (Mal 1:4–5).

13581.text: thought he would come out → angry → went away → servants' question → dipped → flesh restored (2Ki 5:11–14); angry with the priests → leprosy broke out (2Ch 26:19); Naboth's word → vexed and sullen → lay down, turned away his face, ate no food (1Ki 21:4).

13605.text: Face 5F. The great day: the wrath of the Lamb; your wrath came: Hits / verses: 4 / 4; Toward: the kings of the earth and everyone, slave and free; the nations; this people; Other parties named: the mountains and rocks; the dead; the servants, prophets and saints; Example verses: Rev 6:16–17; Rev 11:18; Luk 21:23.

13628.text: orgē (35): God: 29 (the Lamb's in Rev 6:16); Jesus: 1 (Mar 3:5); People: 5 (Eph 4:31; Col 3:8; 1Ti 2:8; Jam 1:19, 20); Other: —; What the count shows: God's wrath in 29 of 35. The same noun is the anger people are told to put away.

13636.text: What meets it (new cases): a father who comes out (Luk 15:28); Jesus's teaching on serving (Mat 20:25–26); a question from their own practice (Luk 13:15; Joh 7:23); a Pharisee's counsel (Act 5:34–35); a chamberlain persuaded (Act 12:20); one another's daily exhortation (Heb 3:13): Verses: as listed.

13642.text: F.6: What emerged: What meets anger decides its end, in the Gospels: the father who comes out (Luk 15:28); the teaching on serving (Mat 20:25–26); a question from their own practice (Luk 13:15); Gamaliel's counsel (Act 5:34).; What it changes elsewhere: Extends unit 4 F.6. Overview part D.; Where: overview D.

13651.text: go astray in their heart → provoked → swore in my wrath → shall not enter (Heb 3:10–11); exhort one another every day → none hardened (3:13); unable to enter because of unbelief (3:19).

13670.text: heard → indignant at the two → Jesus called them → whoever would be great must be your servant (Mat 20:24–26).

13723.text: 2Ki 5:11-14: Naaman "was angry and went away ... turned and went away in a rage"; his inner thought is quoted ("Behold, I thought that he would surely come out"); the servants talk him round (5:13), and "his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child" (5:14): rage, persuasion, obedience, restoration, with no seat word anywhere.

13734.text: Whose seat the anger points to, The heart that provokes the anger (human, the cause): genuine links Rom 2:5 "your hard and impenitent heart … storing up wrath"; Heb 3:10 "always go astray in their heart"; 1Ki 11:9 "his heart had turned away"; 2Ch 32:25 "his heart was proud"; Zec 7:12 "hearts diamond-hard"; Jer 4:4 "foreskin of your hearts"; Isa 57:17; Pro 19:3 "his heart rages against the Lord". What it implies for the no-seat verses: The long series "the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel" (Num 25:3; Judg 2:14, 20; 3:8; 10:7; 2Ki 13:3 …) and "provoking the Lord to anger" (ka'as H3707: 1Ki 14–16; 2Ki 17, 21; Jer 7, 25, 32, 44) carry the human inner cause by narrative: idolatry, turning, stubbornness. The seat is implicit in the offender, and the anger is its answer. Jer 7:19, "Is it I whom they provoke? … Is it not themselves, to their own shame?", turns the provocation back onto the provokers' own inner being.

13741.text: Anger with an act: Moses "saw the calf ... anger burned hot, and he threw the tablets" (Exo 32:19); Balaam struck the donkey (Num 22:27); Balak "struck his hands together" (Num 24:10); Saul's verbal assault on Jonathan (1Sa 20:30); David's verdict on the rich man, "the man who has done this deserves to die" (2Sa 12:5), which the next verse turns: "You are the man."

13754.text: A human seat is hardened by the person, or with no agent named (68 verses): Pharaoh by himself (Exo 8:15, 32; 9:34); the stiff neck (Exo 32:9 ... Neh 9:29; Jer 7:26; 17:23; 19:15); sherirut, "the stubbornness of their evil heart" (Jer 3:17; 7:24; 9:14; 11:8; 13:10; 16:12; 18:12; 23:17; Deu 29:19); "diamond-hard" hearts (Zec 7:12); Nebuchadnezzar's "spirit was hardened" (Dan 5:20); the New Testament hardness of heart (Mat 19:8; Mar 3:5; 6:52; 8:17; 10:5; 16:14; Rom 2:5; Eph 4:18); Psa 95:8 and its New Testament reuse (Heb 3:8, 13, 15; 4:7).

13767.text: The hardening in Psa 95:8, and in its New Testament reuse (Heb 3-4), is human.

13773.text: Lam 3: "He has made my chains heavy ... he shuts out my prayer ... He is a bear lying in wait for me" (3:7-10); the same poem then says "the Lord will not cast off forever, for, though he cause grief, he will have compassion according to the abundance of his steadfast love; for he does not afflict from his heart" (3:31-33): the chains are felt as heavy, and the poet confesses that the affliction does not come from God's heart; here the action and the heart are explicitly not the same.

13793.text: Meribah as a place name: the verses about the people's quarrel are human (Exo 17:7; Num 20:13, 24; 27:14; Deu 32:51); in Deu 33:8 and Psa 81:7 God does the striving or testing, and these are divine; the pure boundary markers (Eze 47:19; 48:28) have no inner being.

13838.text: Rev 6:16 (5F The great day of wrath: the wrath of the Lamb; your wrath came): hide us from the wrath of the Lamb.

13897.text: Fear and anger follow one another: anger at God, then fear of God (2Sa 6:8–9); fear first, then anger at a weaker target (Dan 11:30).

13907.text: Gen 41:8 "his spirit was troubled". Genuine. The bearer's own (Pharaoh's), though in a different scene from his anger. The same king appears once with an angry act and once with a troubled spirit. The seat word comes with the trouble, not with the anger.

14007.text: Psa 10:13 "say in his heart". The offender's.

14008.text: rebels refusing to come: "We will not come up" (Num 16:12–14).

14126.text: Psa 79:6 is followed by "Do not remember against us our former iniquities" (79:8).

14172.text: Daniel's confession resting on mercy, not righteousness (Dan 9:18).

14184.text: How it co-exists: With a murder plan spoken inwardly: "Esau said to himself, '… then I will kill my brother Jacob'" (Gen 27:41). And Rebekah's reading of it: "your brother Esau comforts himself about you by planning to kill you" (27:42). The anger is kept going by a plan that soothes it; With the refusal to cry out: "they do not cry for help when he binds them" (Job 36:13). Cherished anger shuts off the cry; Rebekah's movement is the counter-weight: removing the object (flight) and waiting for the anger's course to end. Her own inner state follows at once: "Why should I be bereft of you both in one day?" (27:45), and "I loathe my life" (27:46).

14190.text: (b) Thwarted and made a fool of: Balaam: "Balaam's anger was kindled, and he struck the donkey with his staff" (Num 22:27). When the donkey speaks, he gives his reason: "Because you have made a fool of me. I wish I had a sword in my hand, for then I would kill you" (22:29). The anger is about being shamed, and it wishes to kill; Balak: "Balak's anger was kindled against Balaam, and he struck his hands together … 'I called you to curse my enemies, and behold, you have blessed them these three times'" (Num 24:10). It ends in dismissal and the withholding of honour: "the Lord has held you back from honor" (24:11); Naaman: "Naaman was angry and went away, saying, 'Behold, I thought that he would surely come out to me …'" (2Ki 5:11), and "he turned and went away in a rage" (5:12). What the anger releases is a disappointed expectation of honour, quoted as his own thought. Pilot §1.4 read the whole movement: rage → persuasion → obedience → restoration; The Ephraimite army, discharged, "became very angry with Judah and returned home in fierce anger" (2Ch 25:10), and later "raided the cities of Judah" (25:13). Anger at being sent away returns as violence against those who sent it.

14192.text: (d) Refused by a subordinate, or exposed: Vashti's refusal: "the king became enraged, and his anger burned within him" (Est 1:12). The counsellor at once generalises the fear to every household: "there will be contempt and wrath in plenty" (1:18). One refusal is read as a threat to the whole order of husbands, and answered by decree (1:19–20); The king of Syria, whose plans Elisha keeps disclosing: "the mind of the king of Syria was greatly troubled because of this thing" (2Ki 6:11). He suspects a traitor: "Will you not show me who of us is for the king of Israel?" (6:11). The servant's answer shows how completely he is exposed: Elisha "tells the king of Israel the words that you speak in your bedroom" (6:12).

14193.text: How it co-exists: With a prior high state: Uzziah "when he was strong, he grew proud" (2Ch 26:16), and the king's "heart … merry with wine" (Est 1:10). Anger comes where a lifted state is checked. F v4 §7 already read Est 1:10 as "the merry heart as the threshold"; this adds Uzziah; With striking (Num 22:27; 24:10, hands; 2Ch 16:10), and with going away (2Ki 5:12; 2Ch 25:10).

14195.text: Seat: In the verse: 2Ki 6:11 "mind" (lev). The bearer's own. Genuine. A v3 §2.1 read it as "the mind [heart] of the king … troubled [sāʿar, storm]". H v1 §1.1 read it as "the most powerful heart is the least its own". Both stand. New here: in this phenomenon the heart's storm is the anger of exposure. What troubles it is that its bedroom words are known (6:12); Outside the verse:; Before:; 2Ch 16:9 "those whose heart is blameless toward him". Genuine. It is the seer's diagnosis just before Asa's rage. The rage is at being told where his heart failed; 2Ch 26:16 "grew proud" (gāvah lēv, the heart high). Genuine. The bearer's own, and it comes before the anger; Est 1:10 "heart … merry". Genuine; Beside: Num 24:13, Balaam: "to do either good or bad of my own will [heart]". Genuine, but the other party's. Balak's anger meets a heart subordinated to the word; 2Ki 5:10, 14 "flesh" is Naaman's skin restored. Spurious as a seat (D v2 R3).

14199.text: What it does to those beneath it: Pleading against it before it rises:; Judah: "let not your anger burn against your servant, for you are like Pharaoh himself" (Gen 44:18). The plea is a long retelling of the father's love (44:19–21 onward); Rachel: "Let not my lord be angry that I cannot rise before you, for the way of women is upon me" (Gen 31:35). The plea for no anger covers a concealment: she is sitting on the stolen gods (31:34); Reading it as a sign: "If he says, 'Good!' it will be well with your servant, but if he is angry, then know that harm is determined by him" (1Sa 20:7). Saul's anger is to be read as the evidence of Saul's intent. Jonathan's knowledge follows the same path: after the spear, "Jonathan knew that his father was determined to put David to death" (20:33); Anticipating it and scripting a reply: Joab to the messenger: "if the king's anger rises, and if he says to you, 'Why did you go so near the city?' … then you shall say, 'Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also'" (2Sa 11:20–21). The anger is foreseen, and so is the one sentence that will turn it. That sentence works because the king had wanted Uriah dead. The line manages the king's anger by exposing the king's own secret; Plotting against it from below: "Bigthan and Teresh … became angry and sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus" (Est 2:21). This is anger rising from the servants, discovered through Mordecai (2:22); Anger acting covertly: Zebul, "when [he] heard the words of Gaal … his anger was kindled. And he sent messengers to Abimelech secretly" (Judg 9:30–31). Anger turned into an ambush plan, "set an ambush in the field" (9:32); A group overrules its king: "the commanders of the Philistines were angry with him … 'Send the man back … how could this fellow reconcile himself to his lord?'" (1Sa 29:4). The king Achish yields: "Nevertheless, the lords do not approve of you" (29:6). The anger comes from suspicion: they fear a loyalty they cannot see.

14203.text: Seat: In the verse: Est 7:7 "life" (nephesh): "Haman stayed to beg for his life". The other party's. Life-sense only. C v3 §7.5 read it under "the soul-life hunted". In this phenomenon the seat word names what the powerful one's anger puts at stake in the one beneath, as M20 §2's Seat found for the hunted; Outside the verse:; Est 7:5 "dared" (literally "whose heart has filled him to do this"). The offender's heart, as the king asks about it. Genuine. New here (no batch cites it). The king's wrath two verses later is aimed at the heart that dared; 1Sa 20:4 "Whatever you say [your soul says], I will do for you". Genuine. The other party's (David's), pledged to by Jonathan. New here. It stands three verses before 1Sa 20:7: Jonathan binds himself to David's soul just before they plan how to read Saul's anger. This adds to F v4 §1.1 (Jonathan and David) without changing it; Gen 41:8 "his spirit was troubled". Genuine. The bearer's own (Pharaoh's), though in a different scene from his anger. The same king appears once with an angry act and once with a troubled spirit. The seat word comes with the trouble, not with the anger.

14238.text: Where it comes from. Disobedience to a given word: "they did not listen to Moses" (Exo 16:20); the calf (32:19); the sin offering burned instead of eaten (Lev 10:16); the women of Midian spared "on Balaam's advice" (Num 31:14–16); the king striking only three times (2Ki 13:18); rebels refusing to come: "We will not come up" (Num 16:12–14).

14240.text: What it does: It tests God with a question: "they tested the Lord by saying, 'Is the Lord among us or not?'" (Exo 17:7); It nearly turns on the leader: "They are almost ready to stone me" (17:4); In the Numbers and Deuteronomy verses, Meribah is where the leaders themselves "rebelled against my command" (Num 20:24), "failing to uphold me as holy … before their eyes" (27:14), and "broke faith with me" (Deu 32:51).

14241.text: How it co-exists: With naming: the place becomes a memory. "He called the name of the place Massah and Meribah" (Exo 17:7), and "These are the waters of Meribah" (Num 20:13); With death sentences on the leaders, repeated at every mention: Aaron "shall not enter the land" (20:24), Moses "gathered to your people" (27:13), "die on the mountain" (Deu 32:50).

14246.text: What it does: "David was angry because the Lord had broken out against Uzzah" (2Sa 6:8 = 1Ch 13:11); "the anger of the Lord blazed hotly, and Moses was displeased" (Num 11:10); "'I regret that I have made Saul king' … And Samuel was angry, and he cried to the Lord all night" (1Sa 15:11).

14262.text: Part 2 verses: the prophet as the vessel of God's anger, plus human wrath taken up into God's praise: Filled, and worn out by holding it: "I am full of the wrath of the Lord; I am weary of holding it in" (Jer 6:11). The cause is the hearers' closed ears: "their ears are uncircumcised, they cannot listen … the word of the Lord is to them an object of scorn" (6:10). The wrath fills the prophet because the word it belongs to has nowhere to go; Filled after being fed: "Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart" (Jer 15:16). Then "I sat alone, because your hand was upon me, for you had filled me with indignation" (15:17), and "Why is my pain unceasing, my wound incurable?" (15:18); The same words that delighted the heart fill the prophet with indignation and isolate him. The next movement is God's call to return (15:19) and a promise: "I will make you … a fortified wall of bronze … I am with you" (15:20); Carried by the Spirit, in the heat of his own spirit: "The Spirit lifted me up and took me away, and I went in bitterness in the heat of my spirit, the hand of the Lord being strong upon me. And I came to the exiles … and I sat there overwhelmed among them seven days" (Eze 3:14–15); Two spirits in one verse: the Spirit that carries, and the prophet's own spirit, heated; The heat ends in seven days of silence among the people before the word comes again (3:16); Across the three prophets, God's anger in the human does not come out as violence. It comes out as weariness (Jer 6:11), isolation and pain (Jer 15:17–18), bitterness and being overwhelmed (Eze 3:14–15). The human bearing of divine anger is suffering, not action. Compare Samson and Saul (Judg 14:19; 1Sa 11:6), whose Spirit-linked anger acted. Those were deliverers; these are prophets; Human wrath taken up into God's praise: "Surely the wrath of man shall praise you; the remnant of wrath you will put on like a belt" (Psa 76:10, B2). Human wrath is neither aligned with God's nor exceeding it. It is used by God. This is a fourth relation, beside §15's aligned (Phinehas), exceeding (2Ch 28:9) and following (Samson). The context is God "who cuts off the spirit of princes".

14263.text: Seat : In the verse: Eze 3:14 "Spirit" (divine, received) + "spirit" (the bearer's own. Genuine); Outside the verse: Jer 15:16 "the delight of my heart". Genuine. The bearer's own. The heart that delighted in the words is the same person filled with indignation in the next verse. Pilot §2.3 noted this; it is confirmed here.

14276.text: Part 2 verses: what they add: The body's end of rivalrous anger: "The wicked man sees it and is angry; he gnashes his teeth and melts away; the desire of the wicked will perish!" (Psa 112:10). What he sees is the righteous man, whose "horn is exalted in honor" (112:9). Seeing the rival's rise ends in the angry one dissolving, not in the spear of 1Sa 18; Contrast seat: "His heart is steady; he will not be afraid" (112:8), said of the righteous one, two verses before. The seat is again named in the one the anger is aimed at (see Neh 4:6 above). Genuine; Rivalry among the disciples: "when the ten heard it, they were indignant at the two brothers" (Mat 20:24 = Mar 10:41). What they heard was Jesus's answer about the two brothers' place: "to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to grant" (Mat 20:23; Mar 10:40); Jesus answers by redefining greatness: "You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them … It shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant" (Mat 20:25–26; Mar 10:42–43); The anger at a rival's rise is not rebuked directly. The standing it is about is re-defined, so the rise it resented no longer counts. This is a reframing, the §9 and §6 move used on rivalry; Seat : none in-verse.

14318.text: How it co-exists: With stopping the ears: "they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him" (Act 7:57). The rage refuses to go on hearing; With a calm figure beside it: "But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God" (Act 7:55). And "passing through their midst, he went away" (Luk 4:30). The seat is again named in the contrast figure; With counsel that restrains it: Gamaliel, "if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found opposing God!" (Act 5:39). They "took his advice", and yet "beat them" (5:40). Restrained from killing, but not from beating.

14370.text: Gen 27:41–45: Sequence the text gives: the blessing lost → hatred → murder planned in his heart (ESV "said to himself"; Hebrew in his heart), comforting himself → flight → waiting until the anger "turns away" and he "forgets".

14378.text: 2Sa 6:7–10 = 1Ch 13:10–13: Sequence the text gives: God strikes Uzzah → David angry at God → David afraid of God → avoidance (the ark set aside).

14382.text: 2Ki 5:11–14: Sequence the text gives: expectation ("I thought") → anger → rage, going away → servants' persuasion → obedience → flesh restored.

14392.text: (v2) Jer 15:16–20: Sequence the text gives: words eaten → delight of my heart → sitting alone → filled with indignation → unceasing pain → call to return → "a fortified wall … I am with you".

14399.text: (v2) Luk 15:25–32: Sequence the text gives: music heard → the servant explains → angry, refuses to go in → the father comes out and entreats → the ledger ("these many years") → "this son of yours" → "this your brother" → (no answer).

14406.text: 2Ki 6:11: Seat word (Strong's as tagged): "mind" lev (H3820A); Phenomenon: TH §4; Whose seat: the bearer's own; Seat-sense check: genuine: the storm of exposure; Already read in: A v3 §2.1; H v1 §1.1.

14433.text: Genuine: the bearer's own: Verses: 2Ki 6:11; Est 5:9; Job 18:4; Job 36:13; (v2) Psa 31:9; Psa 95:8; Pro 6:14; 14:29; 16:32; 19:3; Ecc 2:23; 7:3; 7:9; 11:10; Isa 7:4; Eze 3:14 (own spirit); Eze 32:9; Act 7:54; 17:16; Count: 19.

14440.text: Gen 41:10 (PW): Context verse: Gen 41:8 "his spirit was troubled"; Whose seat · sense: bearer's own (Pharaoh) · genuine; Batch: A v3 §3.2; B v3 §7; Used in: §5.

14444.text: Num 24:10 (TH): Context verse: Num 24:13 "my own will" [heart]; Whose seat · sense: other party's (Balaam) · genuine; Batch: D v2 §2.6; Used in: §4.

14453.text: 2Ki 5:11–12 (TH): Context verse: 2Ki 5:10, 14 "flesh"; Whose seat · sense: bodily · spurious; Batch: D v2 R3; Used in: §4.

14470.text: VX §8 (Psa 10:14; 31:9; Ecc 1:18; 2:23; 7:3; 11:10; Col 3:21; Eph 6:4): Context seats: sense · batch · use: Psa 10:13 "say in his heart": offender's · C v3 §9.4 · used. Psa 31:7 "distress of my soul": bearer's own · E v2 §10.1 · used. Ecc 1:16–17 heart · E v2 §1.3, B v3 §1.2 · used. Ecc 2:22 heart · new · used. Ecc 2:24 "find" [make his soul see good] · new · used (enjoyment as answer). Ecc 5:16 "wind" · spurious. Ecc 7:2, 7:4 heart · A v3 §3.3 · used. Ecc 11:9 heart · F v4 §7, H v1 §4.1 · used. Eph 6:5–6, Col 3:22–23 "heart … heartily" (bondservants) · E v2 §6, H v1 §3.1 · not used (next household rule).

14473.text: SP §15 (Jer 15:17; Eze 3:14; Psa 76:10): Context seats: sense · batch · use: Jer 15:16 heart · A v3 §4.2 · used. Eze 3:12 "Spirit" · divine · new · context of 3:14. Psa 76:12 "spirit of princes" · H v1 §1.1 · used.

14499.text: What it does: Sung by the rescued: "you send out your fury; it consumes them like stubble" (Exo 15:7); Promised to the obedient: "if you carefully obey his voice … then I will be an enemy to your enemies and an adversary to your adversaries" (Exo 23:22); Released by the cry of the weak: "If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to me, I will surely hear their cry, and my wrath will burn" (Exo 22:23–24); Released by the psalmist's call: "In my distress I called upon the Lord … my cry came to his ears. Then the earth reeled … because he was angry" (2Sa 22:7–8).

14500.text: Where it comes from. From the human cry: the widow's and orphan's (Exo 22:23), the poor debtor's (22:27: "if he cries to me, I will hear, for I am compassionate"), David's "in my distress" (2Sa 22:7). In two of the four verses, the human cry is what precedes the anger.

14502.text: Part B: Psa 7:11; 18:7; 21:9; 78:49; 78:50; 110:5; Isa 30:27; 30:30; 66:14; 66:15: Psa 18:7 is the psalm text of 2Sa 22:8: "In my distress I called upon the Lord … because he was angry" (Psa 18:6–7); The upright in heart, and the call to repent. "God is a righteous judge, and a God who feels indignation every day" (Psa 7:11). This follows "you who test the minds and hearts … who saves the upright in heart" (7:9–10), and is followed by "If a man does not repent, God will whet his sword" (7:12). The protection is for the upright in heart, and the indignation waits on repentance; The king who trusts: "the king trusts in the Lord … Your hand will find out all your enemies" (Psa 21:7–9). The king at God's right hand: "Your people will offer themselves freely" (110:3, 5); The Exodus retold: "He made a path for his anger; he did not spare them from death" (Psa 78:50). "Then he led out his people like sheep" (78:52); The protected rejoice in the heart; "You shall have a song … and gladness of heart" (Isa 30:29), while "the Assyrians will be terror-stricken" (30:31); "As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you … You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice; your bones shall flourish like the grass" (66:13–14); The protected are the people the anger struck earlier: "the Lord binds up the brokenness of his people, and heals the wounds inflicted by his blow" (Isa 30:26); Seat ; In the verse: Isa 66:14 "your heart shall rejoice". The comforted people's own. Genuine. Psa 78:50 "them" (nephesh) is the Egyptians' life. Life-sense; Outside: Psa 7:9–10 "hearts" / "upright in heart". Isa 30:29 "gladness of heart"; What part B adds. Part A had only praise (Exo 15). Part B places the joy of the protected in the heart.

14503.text: Part C: Eze 36:6; Nah 1:2; Hab 3:8; 3:12; Zec 8:2: Anger for the reproached: "Behold, I have spoken in my jealous wrath, because you have suffered the reproach of the nations" (Eze 36:6). Edom took the land "with wholehearted joy and utter contempt" (36:5). "you will soon come home" (36:8); "I am jealous for Zion with great jealousy, and I am jealous for her with great wrath. … I have returned to Zion" (Zec 8:2–3). "The Lord … keeps wrath for his enemies" (Nah 1:2); Habakkuk's prayer, from inside the fear:; "O Lord, I have heard the report of you, and your work, O Lord, do I fear … in wrath remember mercy" (Hab 3:2); "Was your wrath against the rivers …? … You went out for the salvation of your people" (3:8, 13); the enemy came "rejoicing as if to devour the poor in secret" (3:14); then: "I hear, and my body trembles; my lips quiver … rottenness enters into my bones … Yet I will quietly wait for the day of trouble to come upon people who invade us" (3:16); and: "Though the fig tree should not blossom … yet I will rejoice in the Lord" (3:17–18).

14510.text: Part C: Eze 9:8; Dan 9:16; Zec 1:12: The prophet refused. "while they were striking, and I was left alone, I fell upon my face, and cried, 'Ah, Lord God! Will you destroy all the remnant of Israel …?'" (Eze 9:8). The answer is no: "The guilt … is exceedingly great … For they say, 'The Lord has forsaken the land, and the Lord does not see.' As for me, my eye will not spare" (9:9–10). Some are spared: the mark is put "on the foreheads of the men who sigh and groan over all the abominations" (9:4, context read). Those who grieve over the sin are marked. The one who pleads for the rest is not answered; Daniel's confession-intercession:; "O Lord, according to all your righteous acts, let your anger and your wrath turn away from your city Jerusalem … because for our sins, and for the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem … [has] become a byword" (Dan 9:16); "the Lord our God is righteous in all the works that he has done" (9:14); "for your own sake" (9:17); "we do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy" (9:18); An angel intercedes: "O Lord of hosts, how long will you have no mercy on Jerusalem …, against which you have been angry these seventy years?" This is answered with "gracious and comforting words" (Zec 1:12–13).

14518.text: How it co-exists: The breaking out stops a celebration. "David and all the house of Israel were celebrating before the Lord" (2Sa 6:5; 1Ch 13:8); It produces anger at God, then fear of God. "David was angry … David was afraid of the Lord that day … 'How can the ark of the Lord come to me?'" (2Sa 6:8–9; 1Ch 13:11–12). This is U1 §13 and §37; (New here, from context.) The fear is resolved by seeing blessing on someone else. "The Lord blessed Obed-edom and all his household … So David went and brought up the ark … with rejoicing" (2Sa 6:11–12). David does not reason his way past the fear. He watches another household live with the ark.

14528.text: What it does: Complaint: "the people complained in the hearing of the Lord about their misfortunes, and when the Lord heard it, his anger was kindled" (Num 11:1); Craving: "While the meat was yet between their teeth … the anger of the Lord was kindled" (Num 11:33). The place is named after it: "there they buried the people who had the craving" (11:34). Already read in A v3 §2.2 ("craving and anger"); Unbelief: "Yet in spite of this word you did not believe the Lord your God … And the Lord heard your words and was angered" (Deu 1:32–34); Discouraging the heart: the spies "discouraged the heart of the people of Israel from going into the land" (Num 32:9), and "the Lord's anger was kindled on that day" (32:10).

14534.text: Part C: Heb 3:10; 3:11; 3:17; 4:3: Hebrews reads Psalm 95 to a new audience:; "Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart, leading you to fall away from the living God. But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called 'today,' that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin" (Heb 3:12–13); "So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief" (3:19); "let us fear lest any of you should seem to have failed to reach it" (4:1); "we who have believed enter that rest" (4:3); The wilderness provocation is made a daily warning, kept by exhorting one another — part A's "remember and do not forget" (Deu 9:7) in a new form; Seat ; In the verse: Heb 3:10 "go astray in their heart". The fathers'. Genuine; Outside: Heb 3:8, 15 "do not harden your hearts"; 3:12 "evil, unbelieving heart".

14543.text: Where it comes from. From going after a permission hedged with "only do what I tell you" (22:20).

14555.text: Part B: Psa 81:7. "In distress you called, and I delivered you; I answered you in the secret place of thunder; I tested you at the waters of Meribah." Then: "O Israel, if you would but listen to me!" (81:8): A second text reads Meribah as God's test (with Deu 33:8). Here the test stands beside a deliverance, and is recalled to call Israel to listen.

14558.text: What it leads to. The offender removed ("Why did you bring trouble on us? The Lord brings trouble on you today", Jos 7:25), a heap of stones, "Then the Lord turned from his burning anger" (7:26). The misunderstanding over the altar is resolved (22:21–23 onward).

14602.text: Part B: Psa 56:7; 59:13; 69:24; 79:6; Jer 10:25; 18:23; Lam 3:66 (seven verses). The imprecation is a recurring form in part B, as part A's pointer expected: The grounds given:; enemies who "injure my cause … have waited for my life" (Psa 56:5–6); "the sin of their mouths … the cursing and lies" (59:12); "they persecute him whom you have struck down, and they recount the pain of those you have wounded" (69:26): they add to God's striking; "the nations that do not know you … have devoured Jacob" (79:6–7; Jer 10:25 in the same words); Restraint inside the imprecation: "Kill them not, lest my people forget … consume them in wrath … that they may know that God rules over Jacob" (Psa 59:11, 13). The purpose given is knowledge; Tears and trust beside it: "put my tears in your bottle … This I know, that God is for me" (56:8–9); Paired with the speaker's own plea against anger:; Psa 79:6 is followed by "Do not remember against us our former iniquities" (79:8); Jer 10:25 is preceded by "Correct me, O Lord … not in your anger"; The one who asks for wrath on the nations asks to be corrected without it; The intercessor turned imprecator; "Remember how I stood before you to speak good for them, to turn away your wrath from them" (Jer 18:20); Three verses later: "Forgive not their iniquity … deal with them in the time of your anger" (18:23); The one who turned the anger away now asks for it, because good was repaid with evil: "they have dug a pit for my life" (18:20). See §45; Lam 3:66 comes with "You will give them dullness of heart" (3:65); Seat ; In the verse: none; Outside: Lam 3:65 "dullness of heart". The enemies'. Genuine. Psa 56:6 "my life" (nephesh). Life-sense.

14610.text: How it co-exists: Isolation. "He has put my brothers far from me … My relatives have failed me, my close friends have forgotten me" (19:13–14). "Men have gaped at me with their mouth" (16:10); Not being able to see God. "Behold, he passes by me, and I see him not" (9:11). "If I summoned him and he answered me, I would not believe that he was listening to my voice" (9:16); A wish not to have been born. "Why did you bring me out from the womb?" (10:18). "leave me alone, that I may find a little cheer" (10:20); Hope beyond the anger, in the same breath. "Oh that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would conceal me until your wrath be past, that you would appoint me a set time, and remember me! … You would call, and I would answer you; you would long for the work of your hands" (14:13, 15). Job asks for a hiding place from God's anger in God's own keeping, and expects God to long for him afterwards.

14613.text: Part B: Psa 88:7; 88:16; 102:10: Psalm 88, like Job, gives no cause. "Your wrath lies heavy upon me, and you overwhelm me with all your waves" (88:7); "Your wrath has swept over me; your dreadful assaults destroy me" (88:16); "Afflicted and close to death from my youth up" (88:15); Isolation: "You have caused my companions to shun me; you have made me a horror to them" (88:8); "my companions have become darkness" (88:18); Not seeing God: "O Lord, why do you cast my soul away? Why do you hide your face from me?" (88:14); Calling continues: "Every day I call upon you, O Lord; I spread out my hands to you" (88:9); Unlike Job, Psalm 88 has no turn. Its last verse (88:18) ends in darkness; Psa 102:10: "For I eat ashes like bread and mingle tears with my drink, because of your indignation and anger; for you have taken me up and thrown me down" (102:9–10). His enemies "use my name for a curse" (102:8). Then "But you, O Lord, are enthroned forever" (102:12); Seat . Outside: Psa 88:14 "cast my soul away". The bearer's own. Genuine. Pilot §2 (second row) cites Psa 88:7, 16.

14629.text: How it co-exists: Security broken first: "As for me, I said in my prosperity, 'I shall never be moved.' … you hid your face; I was dismayed" (Psa 30:6–7); Fear removed: "be not afraid of the Assyrians" (Isa 10:24); "I will trust, and will not be afraid" (12:2); Grief addressed: "like a wife deserted and grieved in spirit" (54:6); "O afflicted one, storm-tossed and not comforted" (54:11); Peace offered even to enemies: "let them lay hold of my protection, let them make peace with me" (27:5).

14631.text: Seat: In the verse: none; Outside:; Psa 30:3 "you have brought up my soul from Sheol". The speaker's own. Genuine. Not found in the batches: new as a context seat; Isa 54:6 "grieved in spirit". Zion's. Genuine; Jer 32:39 "one heart". Given by God to the people. Genuine.

14635.text: How it co-exists: Past mercy as the ground: "You forgave the iniquity of your people … You withdrew all your wrath … Restore us again" (Psa 85:2–4); "Will you not revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you?" (85:6); Relationship as the ground:; "the sheep of your pasture" (74:1); "Remember your congregation, which you have purchased of old" (74:2); "you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand … please look, we are all your people" (Isa 64:8–9); Confession, or none; Isa 64 confesses: "you were angry, and we sinned; in our sins we have been a long time, and shall we be saved? … all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment" (64:5–6); Psa 79 asks: "Do not remember against us our former iniquities" (79:8); Psa 89 does not confess. It holds God to his covenant (89:38–39); The anger reaches even prayer:; "angry with your people's prayers" (Psa 80:4); "There is no one who calls upon your name, who rouses himself to take hold of you; for you have hidden your face from us, and have made us melt in the hand of our iniquities" (Isa 64:7).

14645.text: How it co-exists. The human heart has not changed: "Their heart was not steadfast toward him" (Psa 78:37); "they flattered him with their mouths" (78:36); "he went on backsliding in the way of his own heart" (Isa 57:17); "from before birth you were called a rebel" (48:8).

14648.text: Part C: Eze 20:8; 20:13; 20:21; Hos 11:9: Three times in one chapter: "Then I said I would pour out my wrath upon them … But I acted for the sake of my name" (Eze 20:8–9, 13–14, 21–22: "I withheld my hand"). The chapter ends: "you shall remember your ways … and you shall loathe yourselves … when I deal with you for my name's sake, not according to your evil ways" (20:43–44); Hosea gives another reason: "How can I give you up, O Ephraim? … My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender. I will not execute my burning anger … for I am God and not a man" (Hos 11:8–9). The people were "bent on turning away from me" (11:7). They will return "trembling like birds from Egypt" (11:11); The reasons given for restraint now include God's own nature ("God and not a man"), beside human frailty and the name; What the restrained do:; they remember and loathe themselves (Eze 20:43; also 16:63: "that you may remember and be confounded … when I atone for you"); they come trembling (Hos 11:10–11); Seat . Outside: Hos 11:8 "My heart recoils". God's. Divine.

14662.text: Part C: Zep 3:8; Zec 7:12; Mal 1:4: Correction refused: "I said, 'Surely you will fear me; you will accept correction' … But all the more they were eager to make all their deeds corrupt" (Zep 3:7). The next verse (3:8) is wrath on the nations, followed by "a pure speech, that all of them may call upon the name of the Lord" (3:9); The heart made hard against hearing: "they refused to pay attention and turned a stubborn shoulder and stopped their ears … They made their hearts diamond-hard lest they should hear the law … Therefore great anger came" (Zec 7:11–12); Refusal returned in kind: "As I called, and they would not hear, so they called, and I would not hear" (7:13); Rebuilding against the blow, again: "If Edom says, 'We are shattered but we will rebuild the ruins,' the Lord of hosts says, 'They may build, but I will tear down … the people with whom the Lord is angry forever'" (Mal 1:4). This is Isa 9:10's "we will build with dressed stones" said by another nation; Seat . In the verse: Zec 7:12 "hearts diamond-hard". The people's own. Genuine. The same verse has "his Spirit" (God's; divine). Outside: Zec 7:10 "devise evil against another in your heart"; What part C adds. Part B's "heart that does not take it in" was a failure to understand. Zec 7:12 names an act: the heart made hard so as not to hear.

14680.text: Part C: Zep 2:2; 2:3; Rev 6:16: Hiding offered, with "perhaps": "Gather together, yes, gather, O shameless nation, before the decree takes effect … Seek the Lord, all you humble of the land … seek righteousness; seek humility; perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the Lord" (Zep 2:1–3). The way to be hidden is seeking, humility and righteousness, and even then only "perhaps"; Hiding from God, not in him: "the kings of the earth and the great ones … and everyone, slave and free, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains, calling to the mountains and rocks, 'Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb'" (Rev 6:15–16); This is the reverse of Isa 26:20. There God calls his people into their chambers. Here people ask the mountains to hide them from God.

14688.text: Where it comes from. The human side here is an absence: Part A §4 had Moses standing before the anger, and Psa 106:23 says "had not Moses … stood in the breach"; Isa 64:7 gives the people's side of the same absence: "There is no one who calls upon your name, who rouses himself to take hold of you".

14709.text: What it does: "In your forbearance take me not away; know that for your sake I bear reproach" (Jer 15:15); "Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart … I sat alone, because your hand was upon me, for you had filled me with indignation" (15:16–17); "Remember how I stood before you to speak good for them, to turn away your wrath from them" (18:20). The same verse: "they have dug a pit for my life".

14710.text: Where it comes from. From the word eaten (15:16) and the commission.

14713.text: Seat: In the verse: Jer 18:20 "life". The prophet's. Life-sense; Outside:; Jer 15:16 "delight of my heart"; Jer 8:18 "my heart is sick".

14726.text: How it co-exists: The body of the one speaking: "From on high he sent fire; into my bones he made it descend … he has left me stunned, faint all the day long" (1:13); "He has made my flesh and my skin waste away; he has broken my bones" (3:4); "He has walled me about so that I cannot escape; he has made my chains heavy; though I call and cry for help, he shuts out my prayer" (3:7–8); Hunger at its worst: "The hands of compassionate women have boiled their own children" (4:10); "Should women eat the fruit of their womb …?" (2:20); Pouring out the heart: "Arise, cry out in the night … Pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord! Lift your hands to him for the lives of your children" (2:19); "Let us lift up our hearts and hands to God in heaven" (3:41); Hope inside the lament (context of Lam 3:1, read this session):; "My soul continually remembers it and is bowed down within me. But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: The steadfast love of the Lord never ceases" (3:20–22); "For the Lord will not cast off forever, for, though he cause grief, he will have compassion … for he does not afflict from his heart or grieve the children of men" (3:31–33); "Let us test and examine our ways, and return to the Lord!" (3:40); Outsiders' disbelief: "The kings of the earth did not believe … that foe or enemy could enter the gates of Jerusalem" (4:12).

14765.text: What it does: "'Yet even now,' declares the Lord, 'return to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning; and rend your hearts and not your garments.' Return to the Lord your God, for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger … Who knows whether he will not turn and relent, and leave a blessing behind him …?" (Joe 2:12–14); The king of Nineveh: "Let neither man nor beast … taste anything … let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and let them call out mightily to God. Let everyone turn from his evil way and from the violence that is in his hands. Who knows? God may turn and relent and turn from his fierce anger, so that we may not perish" (Jon 3:7–9).

14792.text: How it co-exists: Patience toward the vessels of wrath (9:22); A call that crosses peoples: "even us whom he has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles" (9:24).

14805.text: What it leads to. "It is done!" (16:17); the Word of God on the white horse, "King of kings" (19:13–16).

14818.text: Jos 7; 22:10–34: Sequence the text gives: one man takes → anger on all → defeat → offender removed → anger turns → the memory drives a later confrontation → answer "He knows"; Phenomena: OS · TW.

14830.text: (v2) Isa 57:14–18: Sequence the text gives: God dwells with the contrite spirit → "nor will I always be angry; for the spirit would grow faint before me" → struck, hid face → backsliding "in the way of his own heart" → "I will heal him"; Phenomena: RS.

14831.text: (v2) Isa 63:1–64:12: Sequence the text gives: no one to help → God's arm alone → "I will recount the steadfast love" → "you were angry, and we sinned" → no one who calls → "we are the clay … please look"; Phenomena: NI · CL.

15059.text: Where it would go (not decided). There is no shame or reproach section in the narrative. When the whole set is read, the faces above point to one account of reproach and shame (a new section, its place yours to decide), with parts woven into Ch 4 (the heart broken by reproach), 10.12 (the taunt that makes afraid), 10.10 (taunting and reviling another), 10.9 (reproach laid before God), 13.1 (God reproached; Christ bearing it), and 10.6 / Ch 12 / Ch 7 for Rom 1.

15140.text: Made bold. "On the day I called, you answered me; my strength of soul you increased" (Psa 138:3). The word rāhab is glossed "be assertive". Elsewhere it is "insolent" (Isa 3:5). Here God increases it, in answer to a call.

15150.text: The other face (2Ch 17:6; Psa 138:3) goes to Ch 11 §4 (change of character).

15205.text: Proverbs paints the scoffer by what he will not receive: Rebuke; "A wise son hears his father's instruction, but a scoffer does not listen to rebuke" (Pro 13:1); "A scoffer does not like to be reproved; he will not go to the wise" (15:12). The verse before is "Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the Lord; how much more the hearts of the children of man!" (15:11); Hatred of correction. "Whoever corrects a scoffer gets himself abuse ... Do not reprove a scoffer, or he will hate you; reprove a wise man, and he will love you" (Pro 9:7–8). The same rebuke brings out hate in one and love in the other; Wisdom in vain. "A scoffer seeks wisdom in vain, but knowledge is easy for a man of understanding" (Pro 14:6). He seeks, and does not find; Learning by his fall; "Strike a scoffer, and the simple will learn prudence" (19:25); "When a scoffer is punished, the simple becomes wise" (21:11); The scoffer is not the one who learns. Others learn from what happens to him; Strife. "Drive out a scoffer, and strife will go out, and quarreling and abuse will cease" (Pro 22:10). "the scoffer is an abomination to mankind" (24:9); Justice and the guilt offering; "A worthless witness mocks at justice" (19:28). "Condemnation is ready for scoffers" (19:29); "Fools mock at the guilt offering, but the upright enjoy acceptance" (14:9). They mock the very means of putting guilt right; Delight, and the offer. "How long will scoffers delight in their scoffing ... If you turn at my reproof, behold, I will pour out my spirit to you" (Pro 1:22–23). Scoffing is a delight held on to, and the offer still stands to the one who turns; Alone. "If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; if you scoff, you alone will bear it" (Pro 9:12); The seat. "Blessed is the man who ... nor sits in the seat of scoffers; but his delight is in the law of the Lord" (Psa 1:1–2). The scoffer's seat is set against delight in the law; The warning; "do not scoff, lest your bonds be made strong", then "Give ear, and hear my voice" (Isa 28:22–23). Again the opposite of scoffing is hearing; "the scoffer cease ... who by a word make a man out to be an offender, and lay a snare for him who reproves in the gate" (Isa 29:20–21). The scoffer works against the one who reproves. In the same passage "The meek shall obtain fresh joy in the Lord" (29:19); Wine and company; "Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise" (Pro 20:1); "the princes became sick with the heat of wine; he stretched out his hand with mockers", and "none of them calls upon me" (Hos 7:5, 7); In Job's debates; Zophar: "when you mock, shall no one shame you?" (Job 11:3); Job: "after I have spoken, mock on" (21:3); Elihu: "Beware lest wrath entice you into scoffing" (36:18); I read: the charge of scoffing is thrown between the speakers. As with Eliab in batch 2, the verses do not settle that it is true of Job; "Toward the scorners he is scornful, but to the humble he gives favor" (Pro 3:34, carried). This is the source of Jam 4:6 and 1Pe 5:5.

15230.text: Wisdom: "Because I have called and you refused to listen ... I also will laugh at your calamity; I will mock when terror strikes you" (Pro 1:24–26).

15237.text: A pride word is used of God here. lāʿag "mock" and lîṣ "scorn" are said of God: "the Lord holds them in derision" (Psa 2:4); "you hold all the nations in derision" (Psa 59:8); "Toward the scorners he is scornful" (Pro 3:34); wisdom: "I will mock when terror strikes you" (Pro 1:26); The verses show how God's derision differs from human mocking; Where it comes from. It comes from the one who "sits in the heavens" (Psa 2:4), from the height that batches 1–3 found is his by nature; What it answers. It always answers a rising against him: kings set "against the Lord and against his Anointed" (Psa 2:2), those of whom it says "'Who,' they think, 'will hear us?'" (Psa 59:7), the scorners (Pro 3:34), those who "refused to listen" (Pro 1:24); Whom it never targets. In these verses it is never aimed at the weak, the poor or the sufferer. Human mocking is aimed at exactly those: the poor (Pro 17:5), a father (Pro 30:17), the sufferer (Psa 22:7), builders called "feeble" (Neh 4:2); I read: God's derision is the laughter of the undisputed height at a dispute that cannot succeed. Human mockery is a self-made height looking down on someone made low; God is not mocked. "Do not be deceived: God is not mocked" (Gal 6:7). The mocking of his messengers goes on "until there was no remedy" (2Ch 36:16). This is the batch 1 point again: God's standing is challenged, and is not overturned; The Son is mocked, and does not answer in kind; The one with the undisputed standing is mocked on that very standing: "Hail, King of the Jews!" (Mat 27:29); "He saved others; he cannot save himself" (Mar 15:31); He "made no answer" (Luk 23:9), and he prays "Father, forgive them" (Luk 23:34); I read: in the Son, the majesty of batch 1 does not defend itself against mockery. This is the clearest instance of 13.1 Lowering himself in these words. It joins the batch 1 point that his majesty and his being "delivered into the hands of men" stand side by side (Luk 9:43–44); Mocking exposes a false height. Zion scorns Sennacherib (2Ki 19:21). Elijah mocks a god who does not answer (1Ki 18:27). Here the mocking does not come from pride. It names a claim that is empty.

15251.text: M23 strength: Verses: Jer 51:53, Isa 40:26, Eph 3:18.

15263.text: Given, then held as one's own: 1Co 4:7, and the kings' accounts. This bears on Ch 12 claim C-209, which now has much wider support: Pride against hearing: Jer 13:15–17; Pro 13:10; the scoffer who will not be rebuked (Pro 13:1; 15:12; 9:7–8). This bears on 10.2 Humility and hearing; Presumption: acting where not sent, speaking what was not commanded (Deu 1:43; 18:20). This bears on 10.7; Pride over others: the poor, the widow, the righteous; contempt; mocking the poor (Pro 17:5). This bears on 10.10 and OT-105; The boast moved to God, and boasting in weakness (Jer 9:23–24; 1Co 1:31; 2Co 12:9). This bears on Ch 12 claim C-182 and Ch 11 §4; Pride against love (1Co 8:1; 13:4), against rest (Hab 2:5 against Psa 131:2), and in place of mourning (1Co 5:2); The other face (2Ch 17:6; Psa 138:3; Psa 47:4; Isa 60:15) goes to Ch 11 §4, as a change of character.

15314.text: What it is set against, God answers otherwise: "though the Lord is high, he regards the lowly, but the haughty he knows from afar" (Psa 138:6); God's derision answers only those who rise against him (Psa 2:2–4; 59:7–8; Pro 1:24–26; 3:34). In these verses it is never aimed at the weak.

15316.text: The same words are not pride when the height is given, or turned toward God: "His heart was courageous [lifted up] in the ways of the Lord" (2Ch 17:6), with gābah, the word used of Uzziah's proud heart; "my strength of soul you increased" (Psa 138:3), with rāhab, elsewhere "insolent" (Isa 3:5); the honour God gives (Psa 47:4; Isa 4:2; 60:15; Nah 2:2); the boast in the Lord; "my heart is not lifted up ... I have calmed and quieted my soul" (Psa 131:1–2), set against the arrogant man "never at rest" (Hab 2:5).

15332.text: It always faces someone: "before me" (1Ki 21:29); "before the Lord" (2Ki 22:19); "before the God of his fathers" (2Ch 33:12); "before your God" (Dan 10:12); Zedekiah's failure is put as "He did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet, who spoke from the mouth of the Lord" (2Ch 36:12). Humbling before the prophet is humbling before the word he carries; Most verses in this group name before whom. Of the rest, 2Ch 12:6 and 2Ch 30:11 answer a word just brought, and Lev 26:41 goes with confession (26:40). Isa 58:3–5 is a fast addressed to God.

15336.text: What goes with it: saying "The Lord is righteous" (2Ch 12:6); tearing clothes, sackcloth, fasting, going about "dejectedly" (1Ki 21:27); weeping (2Ki 22:19); entreating and praying (2Ch 33:12–13); fasting and seeking (Ezr 8:21); the condition "humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways" (2Ch 7:14); confession, and making amends for iniquity (Lev 26:40–41).

15344.text: A humbling God does not take knowledge of: Isa 58:3–5: The people ask: "Why have we fasted, and you see it not? Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?"; The answer: "in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers", and "you fast only to quarrel and to fight"; The form is named and set aside: "Is it to bow down his head like a reed, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him?"; The fast God chooses is turned to others: "to loose the bonds of wickedness … to share your bread with the hungry and bring the homeless poor into your house; when you see the naked, to cover him" (58:6–7); Compare Ahab. His sackcloth and fasting were seen and answered (1Ki 21:27–29); I read: the outward acts are the same. What differs, by the two passages, is what goes with them. Ahab acts "when Ahab heard those words", against himself. In Isa 58 the fast is kept alongside self-pleasure and oppression. The humbling that is not taken knowledge of is one that leaves the seen poor unseen (58:7). This joins OT-105; 10.1, 10.7 and 13.1 already cite Isa 58:3, 5. The reading here is for the humbling side.

15375.text: Already cited: 2Ch 12:7, 12:12, 32:26, 33:12 and 2Ki 22:19 (10.13, where humbling turns wrath); 2Ki 22:19, 2Ch 32:26 and Dan 5:19, 22 (Ch 4); Dan 4:17, 37 (13.1); Deu 8:3 (Ch 2); Pro 16:19 (Ch 12); 2Ch 7:14 (Ch 14); Isa 58:3, 5 (10.1, 10.7, 13.1). None is in a section about humbling, because there is none.

15393.text: Set against religious acts in three passages: the fast (Isa 58:3–7, batch 1); offerings (Mic 6:6–8); the house and the sacrifices (Isa 66:1–3, group III).

15429.text: Psa 51:17: "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise.": What it is set against: "For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it; you will not be pleased with a burnt offering" (51:16); What comes before: "Deliver me from bloodguiltiness" (51:14). The spirit and heart are broken over the speaker's own sin; What it is called: "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit". It takes the place of the offering; The next verses: "then will you delight in right sacrifices" (51:19). The offerings are not abolished. They follow the broken heart; This is a fourth passage where what God looks to is set against a religious act. The others are Isa 58:3–7, Mic 6:6–8 and Isa 66:1–3 (batches 1 and 2). In Psa 51 the contrast is the speaker's own, and the next verses take it back up; "Contrite" here is H1794 (M10). "Broken" is H7665 (M24/T3). No M09 word is in the verse.

15489.text: 1Pe 3:8–9: Humility named: "a humble mind"; Beside it: unity of mind, sympathy, brotherly love, "a tender heart"; Against it: "Do not repay evil for evil".

15498.text: What it is joined to inwardly: "conscience" (Rom 13:5); "mindful of God" (1Pe 2:19); "reverence for Christ" (Eph 5:21); "hoped in God", and "do not fear anything that is frightening" (1Pe 3:5–6); in 1Pe 3:1–4 the submission of a wife is set beside "the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit" (batch 4).

15499.text: Under the unjust. "Servants, be subject to your masters with all respect, not only to the good and gentle but also to the unjust. For this is a gracious thing, when, mindful of God, one endures sorrows while suffering unjustly … because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example" (1Pe 2:18–21): Submission here is bearing wrong, with God in mind and Christ as the pattern; Compare Gen 16:9 (batch 1): Hagar told to return and submit to a mistress who had dealt harshly, with "the Lord has listened to your affliction".

15510.text: From this batch: Christ under whom all things are put (1Cor 15:27; Eph 1:22; 1Pe 3:22; Heb 2:5, 8) and the Son himself subject (1Cor 15:28; Luk 2:51); Jesus "made lower" and crowned because of the suffering of death (Heb 2:7, 9). The word G1642 elattoō (T3) is outside the pull. It also stands in "He must increase, but I must decrease" (Joh 3:30). Both are to be checked in the analysis; Christ as the example of submission under wrong (1Pe 2:21); The ground given for submission is Christ ("reverence for Christ", "as to the Lord", "for the Lord's sake"); The OT words read in batches 1–3 carry no submission verb of this kind. The nearest are Gen 16:9 (Hagar told to submit), Psa 81:11 ("Israel would not submit to me") and 2Ch 30:8 ("yield yourselves to the Lord"). The OT side of the analysis is to be checked against those.

15518.text: 1Pe 2:18–21: Ground: "mindful of God"; "Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example".

15542.text: Mar 12:42; Luk 21:3: "a poor widow came and put in two small copper coins". Jesus says she "has put in more than all those who are contributing … For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on" (Mar 12:43–44; Luk 21:3–4): The measure is what is left, not what is given: "out of their abundance" against "out of her poverty … all she had to live on"; In Mark the scene follows directly on the scribes "who devour widows' houses and for a pretense make long prayers" (12:40). The poor widow gives everything at the treasury, while those who devour widows pray at length for show; I read: the verses name no inner word for her. What they give is the measure Jesus sets; Mar 12:38–44 are cited in 10.5 (the long prayers and the widow; M18 group G). The M09 verse 12:42 and the Luke parallel are not.

15555.text: Eight passages have no citation at all: Luk 14:7–14, Luk 18:18–30, 2Ch 30, Joh 12:1–8, Mar 14:3–9, Pro 28:1–6, Luk 21:1–4, Jer 39:9–10.

15608.text: Verses that are a source in the claims register: Count: 4 (Luk 16:22, Psa 34:18, 2Ch 7:14, Phili 2:8).

15626.text: 10.7 (v29 → v30), "The humbling of the soul was not wrong in itself." Isa 58:5 questions the form of the fast, so the verses do not say this. Removed. The passage now reads: "The humbling stood beside oppression in the same people, and it was not what he chooses.".

15627.text: Claim C-188 (from update 141). It said "In four passages" what God looks to is set against a religious act. That counted only the humility passages, and 13.1 Delight gathers more (Isa 1:11–13; Psa 40:6–8; Hos 6:6; Mat 9:13; 12:7). It is restated to name the humility passages "as in the other passages gathered in 13.1".

15634.text: n3: Claim: The offering is weighed by what is inside the one who brings it (I read); Sources: Isa 1:11–13; Psa 40:6–8; 51:16–19; Hos 6:4–6; Mat 9:13; 12:7.

15649.text: In the NT a new ground is named: Christ, and Christ's own way: "Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus" (Phili 2:5); "Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example" (1Pe 2:21); "out of reverence for Christ" (Eph 5:21); "by the meekness and gentleness of Christ" (2Cor 10:1); "learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart" (Mat 11:29).

15660.text: 13.1 already holds Dan 4:17 and 4:37 (Willing), Psa 51:16–17 (Delight), Jam 4:4–6 (Jealousy) and Isa 58:3, 5 (Choosing). None is placed for God's lowering.

15680.text: The verses do not name humility as a feeling. They name: an act, humbling oneself, done "before" God or before his word, with the heart named as where it happens (batch 1 group I); a standing, being humble, lowly or meek: the humble seek God, are taught and favored, and are glad at another's deliverance (batch 2 group I); a quality that is sought and walked in: "seek humility", "walk humbly with your God", "humility comes before honor", with the fear of the Lord, with wisdom and beside listening to reproof (batch 2 group II); a state of the spirit: a lowly and contrite spirit, a broken heart, which God dwells with, looks to, is near to and heals (batches 2 III and 3 I); a place taken among people: the lower seat, the servant, the title refused (Luk 14:7–11; Mat 23:8–12; Pro 25:6–7); something done to a person: God humbles to test and teach (Deu 8), and brings the proud low (batch 1 groups II and III); God's own way: he "looks far down", "your gentleness made me great", "I have been broken over their whoring heart".

15719.text: G0073 (agōn) is not a vice at all but a positive athletic and military metaphor for perseverance. Every one of its 6 verses is Paul or Hebrews describing his own or the believer's faithful effort: fight the good fight of the faith (1 Tim 6:12), I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race (2 Tim 4:7), run with endurance the race that is set before us (Heb 12:1). Nothing in this strong's verse set describes wrongdoing, discord or a moral failure of any kind; its inclusion in the cluster looks like a gloss-text accident (the English word fight) and not a thematic match, a candidate for a cluster_strong review.

15785.text: bagad as a finite verb form, narrating a specific act of treachery rather than labelling a class: individuals dealing treacherously with a specific party (Jer 12:6's brothers, 1 Sam 14:33's people, Judg 9:23's Shechem against Abimelech, Ps 78:57's fathers) and Israel and Judah dealing treacherously with God directly (Hos 6:7, Jer 3:20 twice, Jer 5:11 twice, Isa 48:8 twice, Jer 12:1).

15802.text: G0073 (agon) has real, coherent, human-relevant meaning: a struggle or contest, most often used in the NT as an athletic or perseverance metaphor for faithful endurance: fight the good fight of the faith (1 Tim 6:12), I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race (2 Tim 4:7), run with endurance the race that is set before us (Heb 12:1). None of its 6 occurrences describes a moral failure or an inner disposition toward wrongdoing.

15828.text: After the rebuke, the passage runs through seven sons (1 Sam 16:8-10), each passed over, to the youngest, out with the sheep (16:11-12): a structural point about the passage, the choice reached only after every son who looked fit has been refused.

15848.text: Heart: "his heart rages against the Lord" when folly ruins his way (Pro 19:3); "The godless in heart cherish anger" (Job 36:13); "the mind [heart] of the king of Syria was greatly troubled [*sāʿar*, storm]" (2Ki 6:11)

15870.text: Spirit [H]: "his spirit was troubled" — after dreams (Gen 41:8; Dan 2:1, 3). Dreams trouble the spirit; the brief §6 notes dream words sit in T2.; "Jesus was troubled in his spirit" (Joh 13:21); "deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled" at others' weeping (Joh 11:33); "he sighed deeply in his spirit" (Mar 8:12)

15886.text: His word: "the precepts of the Lord … rejoicing the heart" (Psa 19:8); "Your testimonies … are the joy of my heart" (Psa 119:111); "Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart" (Jer 15:16).

15920.text: Fainting across every component: heart: "the whole heart faint" // "the whole head is sick" (Isa 1:5); Lam 1:22; Psa 61:2; spirit [H]: Psa 142:3; 143:4; "When I remember God, I moan; when I meditate, my spirit faints" (Psa 77:3); soul: "hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them" (Psa 107:5); flesh: "my flesh faints for you" (Psa 63:1); life: "When my life was fainting away, I remembered the Lord, and my prayer came to you" (Jon 2:7) — fainting turns into remembering and prayer; Revisit 2026-09-28: In the same book, Jonah "was faint" under the east wind and asked to die (Jon 4:8). Fainting in ch. 2 turns to prayer; fainting in ch. 4 turns to a death-wish (Batch G §6).; For spirit-fainting in meditation (Psa 77:3), memory works either way: it deepens the fainting (Psa 77) or turns it (Psa 42:6). See Batch F §9.4.; bosom: "their life is poured out on their mothers' bosom" (Lam 2:12)

15922.text: Self-affliction of the nephesh (fasting, Day of Atonement): "you shall afflict yourselves" (Lev 16:29, 31; 23:27, 32; Num 29:7); "Why have we humbled ourselves?" (Isa 58:3, 5); "I afflicted myself with fasting" (Psa 35:13); a vow "to afflict herself" (Num 30:13).

15941.text: Given by God: "I will give them a heart to know me" (Jer 24:7); "I give you a wise and discerning mind [heart]" (1Ki 3:12); "Who has put wisdom in the inward parts or given understanding to the mind?" (Job 38:36); "God … has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge" (2Co 4:6); "having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know" (Eph 1:18)

15966.text: 2.1 "Wise of heart" = skilled ◆: "every skillful craftsman" = *wise of heart* (Exo 35:10, 25; 36:1, 2, 8; 31:6, d0); "whom I have filled with a spirit of skill" (Exo 28:3) [X]; "every craftsman in whose mind [heart] the Lord had put skill, everyone whose heart stirred him up" (Exo 36:2); "whose hearts stirred them to use their skill" (Exo 35:26); [Claude reading] Wisdom in the heart includes craft skill. God puts it there, and the stirred heart puts it to work.

15977.text: 2.7 Flesh, soul and folly: "not many of you were wise according to worldly standards [flesh]" (1Co 1:26); "an appearance of wisdom … of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh" (Col 2:23); "The fool folds his hands and eats his own flesh" (Ecc 4:5); "Fool! This night your soul is required of you" (Luk 12:20); Revisit 2026-09-28 (context Luk 12:16–21, Batch F §3.3): the "fool" has just addressed his own soul ("Soul, … relax, eat, drink, be merry", 12:19). God answers that the soul is required, i.e. on loan.; "his lips are a snare to his soul" (Pro 18:7)

15988.text: Hearing as eating for the soul: "Listen diligently to me, and eat what is good, and delight yourselves [nephesh] in rich food. Incline your ear … hear, that your soul may live" (Isa 55:2–3); cf. "Your words were found, and I ate them" (Jer 15:16; Batch A)

15999.text: Telling the heart: "he told her all his heart" (Judg 16:17–18) — revealing the heart is speech.; Revisit 2026-09-28 (context Judg 16:15–30, Batch G §3.6): Delilah had framed it: "your heart is not with me … you have not told me where your great strength lies" (15).; Telling all the heart = giving away the secret of strength. The sequence runs: soul vexed (16) → heart told (17–18) → strength gone, "the Lord had left him" (19–20) → the Philistines' merry hearts (25) → strength asked for (28) → "let my soul die" (30).

16010.text: Remembering weighs on the soul: "My soul continually remembers it and is bowed down within me" (Lam 3:20); "I have forgotten what happiness is" (Lam 3:17); "These things I remember, as I pour out my soul" (Psa 42:4, 6).; Revisit 2026-09-28 (contexts Psa 42:4–7 and Psa 77:2–4, Batch F §9.4): memory works either way. In Psa 42 remembering is the turn ("My soul is cast down … therefore I remember you"). In Psa 77 remembering God deepens the fainting of the spirit. "Bless the Lord, O my soul, and forget not" (Psa 103:2) is one of the self-addresses to the soul, now found in five settings (Batch F §15; Batch G §3.2).

16011.text: Remembering turns to hope: "this I call to mind [heart], and therefore I have hope" (Lam 3:21).

16038.text: 9. Cross-cutting observations for Batch B [Claude reading]: The heart is the organ of attention, knowing, understanding, storing, remembering and reasoning. Attention is literally *setting the heart*. The heart's hardness is the same thing as failing to hear and understand.; The soul relates to knowledge by *receiving* it (pleasant, sweet, life-giving) and by dwelling on memories (bowed down). The soul can be commanded to remember. Soul-desire can run ahead of knowledge.; The human spirit is the seat of self-knowledge and searching. It knows a person's thoughts, makes understanding possible as God's breath in man, searches after the heart meditates, and perceives others' inner reasoning. A cool spirit (temper) is linked with understanding and restrained speech.; God's Spirit is the true source of knowledge, wisdom, skill, teaching, remembrance and prophecy. The heart or own spirit as a source of prophecy is condemned.; Hearing is the main channel into the inner seat. The ear receives; the heart keeps, understands or refuses. News makes hearts melt, spirits revive and souls refresh. God hears the heart. The "hearing heart" of 1 Kgs 3:9 is confirmed in the tags.; Revisit 2026-09-28: the context reads add two qualifications.; Hearing sometimes needs seeing. Jacob's spirit revives only when he sees the wagons (Gen 45:27, Batch G §2). Elisha receives the spirit on condition of seeing (2Ki 2:10, Batch F §9.5).; What is heard moves between people. Esau's heart-speech is reported (Gen 27:42, Batch F §8.2). A fainthearted soldier melts others (Deu 20:8, Batch F §6).; Word and breath belong together: creative word // breath of his mouth; Spirit and words in the mouth; empty words are "wind".; Flesh appears as a *way of knowing and judging* ("according to the flesh"), set against revelation from the Father and the Spirit.; Soul-ish vs spiritual (§8) is a genuine textual contrast between the soul and spirit orders, and it touches the open question from depiction v1.

16040.text: 1.1 "The breath of life" is shared by all flesh: "the Lord God formed the man of dust … and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature [*nephesh ḥayyâ*]" (Gen 2:7); The same phrase *nephesh ḥayyâ* is used of fish, birds and beasts: Gen 1:20, 21, 24; 2:19; 9:10, 12, 15, 16; Lev 11:10, 46; Eze 47:9.; The flood falls on "all flesh in which is the breath of life" (Gen 6:17; 7:15, 22).; "In his hand is the life of every living thing and the breath of all mankind" (Job 12:10).; [lexical; Claude reading] "Living soul" does not mark man off from the animals lexically. What Gen 2:7 adds is God's own breathing into one creature.

16056.text: Context Judg 15:14–19 — two spirits in five verses: "the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him … his bonds melted" (14) [D1]; A thousand struck with the jawbone (15). (18); "God split open the hollow place … when he drank, his spirit returned, and he revived" (19) [H1]; [Claude reading] The divine Spirit rushes upon Samson for the fight. Then his own spirit runs out with thirst and comes back with water. The victory and the collapse sit side by side. The human spirit is here the life-energy that drains and returns, distinct from the Spirit that empowers.
