16085.text: What the sequences show [Claude reading]: The oath marks adherence at a cost.; Elisha's triple oath is the price of the double spirit.; The Shunammite uses Elisha's own oath against him. Her bitterness of soul becomes a hold on the prophet that he cannot refuse.; Uriah's oath by David's soul is kept against David's wish. The wine that should have lowered his guard fails (a failed threshold — Batch F §7). He dies for keeping it.; The oath by the soul can guard a life while refusing a life. Zedekiah swears secretly by "who made our souls" to spare Jeremiah's life. He then declines the life offered to him (38:17, 20), from fear (38:19). The oath and the refusal are in one conversation.; 1Sa 17:55 stands on the threshold of 18:1. A formal oath by Saul's soul immediately precedes the knitting of Jonathan's soul to David's.; The oath misused: "As the Lord lives, I will run after him and get something from him" (Gehazi, 2Ki 5:20; §13.2).; Revisit (Batch H): God swears by his own soul: "The Lord God has sworn by himself [*his nephesh*]" (Amo 6:8; Jer 51:14; read in Batch D and E). The oath by a *nephesh* is used of God as well as of men.; The oath answers a claim of vengeance. The murderers of Ish-bosheth: "your enemy, who sought your life. The Lord has avenged my lord the king" (2Sa 4:8). David: "As the Lord lives, who has redeemed my life out of every adversity" → he has them killed (4:9–12). The oath on David's own redeemed soul refuses a vengeance done on his behalf (Batch H §1.4).; Revisit (delta) — the oath with death in view: The oath formula frames the nearness of death. "But truly, as the Lord lives and as your soul lives, there is but a step between me and death" (1Sa 20:3). The oath by Jonathan's soul carries David's own peril.; A life pledged for a life. Rahab asks: "swear to me by the Lord … deliver our lives from death" (Jos 2:12–13). The spies answer: "Our life for yours even to death!" (2:14). They do not swear by the Lord's life. They pledge their own *nephesh*.; An oath on a life, broken after a spirit comes (context 1Sa 19:4–12): Jonathan: "he took his life in his hand and struck down the Philistine … Why then will you sin against innocent blood?" (5); "Saul listened … Saul swore, 'As the Lord lives, he shall not be put to death'" (6); War again; David's victory (8); "a harmful spirit from the Lord came upon Saul" (9) [O]

Victory, then the spirit, then the spear break it. This is the pattern of 1Sa 18:8–10 (Batch F §1.1) repeated after an oath.; The king's oath over a son's life (2Sa 14:11; context in §16.6).

16170.text: What answers the wish is seldom death. The answer is food (Elijah; Israel in Exo 16), a question (Jonah), or something to look at (Num 21).; It is granted only twice: to Samson, in one final act, and to Saul, by a hand that is then condemned.; To carry out another's death-wish is still to kill (2Sa 1:14–16).

16176.text: Context Psa 116:1–9 — cry, self-address, deliverance: "The snares of death encompassed me; the pangs of Sheol laid hold on me" (3); "Then I called on the name of the Lord: 'O Lord, I pray, deliver my soul!'" (4); "Return, O my soul, to your rest" (7); "For you have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling" (8); "I will walk before the Lord in the land of the living" (9) *(missing from iba.db; read from the STEP server)*; [Claude reading] The self-address to the soul (Batch F §9.1, §15) stands between the cry (4) and the declared deliverance (8). The soul is told to rest before the deliverance is stated. What follows is walking "in the land of the living". Compare "you have delivered my soul from death … that I may walk before God in the light of life" (Psa 56:13). In both psalms, deliverance from death is for walking before God.

16216.text: "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die" (context Isa 22:12–14): "the Lord God of hosts called for weeping and mourning" (12); "and behold, joy and gladness, killing oxen … eating flesh and drinking wine" (13); "Surely this iniquity will not be atoned for you until you die" (14); [Claude reading] The feast is held against a call to mourn, with death in view. The threshold (Batch F §7) is entered on purpose. What follows is the only verdict in the set that ties atonement to death itself.

16218.text: 14. Cross-cutting observations for Batch G [Claude reading]: The flesh is valued by circumstance: all living beings; mortal life lived by faith; Christ's own flesh; weakness; an orientation opposed to the Spirit. Joh 6 shifts its value within one discourse.; Life-hatred has two faces. The despairing soul of Job, Qohelet and Jonah hates life from exhaustion. The disciple hates it for another's sake (Batch F §3.2). The words overlap; the purpose differs.; Fringe worth keeping: the dead-but-assembled body without breath (Eze 37:8); Jacob's spirit reviving at the sight of wagons (Gen 45:27); Samson's two prayers (Judg 15:18; 16:28); Uriah's oath by the king's soul, kept against the king; the Shunammite turning Elisha's oath on him; Eli reading heart-prayer as drunkenness; "stumbling of heart" averted by Abigail; the lying spirit volunteering in the council; the idol told "Awake" with the verb that stirs Cyrus's spirit; Nebuchadnezzar's heart replaced by a beast's; Elisha's heart going out to meet Naaman's chariot; Isaac's soul blessing after wine; Revisit (delta) — the death side confirms and extends the life side: The inner seat can die before the body. Nabal's heart dies ten days before the Lord strikes him (§16.1).; At death the texts give each component its own verb. The soul "departs" (Rachel). The heart "does not attend" (Phinehas's wife). The spirit is "not retained" (Ecc 8:8) and is "gathered back" (Job 34:14).; *nephesh* names the corpse as well as the living creature (§16.7). What it names is the individual.; The death-wish belongs to the soul, and is seldom answered with death (§16.2, §6).; Food answers Elijah and the people. A question answers Jonah. Something to look at answers the people in Num 21.; It is granted to Samson in one last act. To Saul it is granted by a hand that is condemned for it.; Eating stands at the threshold between wanting to die and going on. This is the life-giving face of the eating threshold in Batch F §7.; The heart decides which death is just (§16.6, §5.4).; The law of refuge tests the killer's past hatred in the heart, and shields him from the avenger's hot heart.; Ransom is refused only for the life that took a life in hatred.; Where the law refuses a price, a mediator "finds a ransom" (Job 33:24). Love cannot be bought at all (Song 8:7).; Deliverance from death is for something (§16.4).

16747.text: What the sequence shows [Claude reading]: Allegiance is a heart-matter, and it moves by attention. Absalom wins hearts by standing where the king is absent (15:2–4) and by the kiss the king himself gave him (14:33 → 15:5). The heart follows whoever hears the cause.; The king's own heart drives the plot. The heart that "went out to Absalom" (14:1) opens the way for the son who steals every other heart. After the victory the same heart grieves, and nearly loses the army (19:6–7).; Flesh as a claim on the heart. David recovers Judah's heart with "bone and flesh" — kinship offered as grounds for allegiance.; The same claim in the opposite direction: Abimelech — "Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh" (Judg 9:2) → "their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, 'He is our brother'" (9:3) → he kills his seventy brothers "on one stone" (9:5).; One appeal to kinship-flesh wins hearts for restoration in one case and for fratricide in the other. [Claude reading]

Only the "rest / settle upon" uses are read in §9.; "show / teach" (H3384B, H2324, G1166, G1731) sits in M05: Exo 35:34; Pro 4:4; Psa 86:11; Hab 2:19; Dan 2:11; 5:12; Rom 2:15.; "sinful" (G0268) sits in M10: Jam 4:8; 5:20; Heb 12:3.; The Lev 11 dietary "detestable" (H8263) sits in M06.; Misfiled but kept, because the context is significant — the "be quiet" pairs (H2790B) in Num 30:4, 7, 11. A father's or husband's silence on hearing lets the vow by which a woman "bound her soul" stand (see §9.5).

16863.text: Night two (context Song 5:2–6): "I slept, but my heart was awake. A sound! My beloved is knocking" (5:2); She delays: "I had put off my garment; how could I put it on?" (5:3); "My beloved put his hand to the latch, and my heart was thrilled within me" (5:4); "I opened … but my beloved had turned and gone. My soul failed me [*went out*] when he spoke. I sought him, but found him not" (5:6)

16864.text: The interaction [Claude reading]: In both nights the soul is the lover and the seeker. The heart, not the soul, is what stays awake and what "thrills".; In Song 5 the heart responds at once, but the body delays (garment, feet). By the time she opens, he is gone, and the soul "goes out".; The components come apart in time: the heart is ready; the body lags; the soul collapses at the lost moment; The same "whom my soul loves" that ends in holding (3:4) ends here in failing (5:6).

16929.text: Judg 16:25–28 | Samson blinded, in prison | "when their hearts were merry, they said, 'Call Samson, that he may entertain us'" (16:25) | Samson calls to the Lord; the house falls (16:28–30)

16932.text: What the pattern shows [Claude reading]: The merry heart is a threshold state. In every narrative it comes after eating and drinking and immediately before a decisive event, which others usually initiate. The good heart lowers guard. What enters at that moment decides the outcome: murder (Amnon); exposure and anger (Vashti, Ahasuerus); mockery turned to catastrophe (Samson); outrage (Gibeah); approach and redemption (Ruth); a dead heart the next morning (Nabal); God's claim on the soul (the rich fool); The heart's condition swings overnight. Nabal: merry heart → dead heart (1Sa 25:36–37). Ahasuerus: merry heart → burning anger (Est 1:10–12). The heart's state is not stable; wine sets it high, and news or refusal drops it.; 1Ki 21 joins spirit and heart. Ahab's spirit is vexed and he stops eating. Jezebel prescribes food and a good heart, secured by injustice. A spirit-state is "cured" by manufacturing a heart-state — the only place in the batch where one is treated through the other.; Positive merriment exists outside the narratives: "they … went to their homes joyful and glad of heart for all the goodness that the Lord had shown" (1Ki 8:66); "A joyful heart is good medicine" (Pro 17:22); "A glad heart makes a cheerful face" (Pro 15:13); "let your heart cheer you … But know that … God will bring you into judgment" (Ecc 11:9); When the heart is good because of God, no threshold event follows. When it is good from wine, one does.; Revisit (Batch G) — the threshold pattern extended: The step before the merry heart: "Strengthen your heart with a morsel of bread" (Judg 19:5, 8). The father-in-law alternates *strengthen* (5, 8) and *merry* (6, 9). Each round delays departure (G §3.1).; The threshold engineered and refused: David "made him drunk" (2Sa 11:13). Uriah, who had sworn "as your soul lives, I will not do this thing" (11:11), still does not go home. The next morning: the death letter (11:14–15) (G §4).; The soul's version: "prepare for me delicious food … that my soul may bless you" (Gen 27:4). "He ate; and he brought him wine, and he drank" (27:25) → the irreversible blessing of the false firstborn → Esau's hatred "in his heart" (27:41; §8.2 below) (G §13.3).; The Samson sequence in full (Judg 16:15–30): soul vexed (16); heart told (17); strength and the Lord gone (19–20); the Philistines' merry hearts (25); strength asked for (28)

16934.text: What the pattern shows [Claude reading]: The threshold entered with death in view: the Lord "called for weeping and mourning … and behold, joy and gladness … eating flesh and drinking wine. 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.'" → "this iniquity will not be atoned for you until you die" (Isa 22:12–14). The feast is held against a call to mourn.; The threshold reversed: Elijah asks to die (1Ki 19:4) → "Arise and eat" (19:5, 7) → "in the strength of that food" to Horeb (19:8). Here the meal does not lower the guard. It carries an exhausted soul across from wanting to die to going on.

16937.text: Context Gen 27:41–42: "Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing … and Esau said to himself [*in his heart*], '… then I will kill my brother Jacob'" (27:41); "But the words of Esau … were told to Rebekah … 'your brother Esau comforts himself about you by planning to kill you'" (27:42)

16972.text: Peace guarding hearts: Context Phili 4:6–7: "do not be anxious … let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God … will guard your hearts and your minds"; "let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts" (Col 3:15); "Peace I leave with you … Let not your hearts be troubled" (Joh 14:27); "In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world" (Joh 16:33)

16988.text: 14. Cross-cutting observations for Batch F [Claude reading]: Relating to others is most often a matter of the soul.; Souls are knit (1Sa 18:1).; A soul loves, seeks and fails (Song 3; 5).; Malice lives in the soul (Eze 25:6, 15).; Souls abhor each other, even God's soul and the people's (Lev 26).; One loves another "as one's own soul".; The heart is where hatred starts and is spoken (Lev 19:17; Gen 27:41). It is also where the response to another's fall is judged (Pro 24:17).; The human spirit registers bonds and bearing.; It is unsettled by a friend's absence and refreshed by a friend's arrival (2Co 2:13; 7:13; 1Co 16:18).; It is the manner of approach — gentleness (1Co 4:21).; It is what the wise hold back and the fool vents (Pro 29:11).; Sequences matter more than single verses. Reading before and after changed the picture in six places: 1Sa 18 (Jonathan and Saul); Lev 26 (reciprocal abhorrence broken by God); Psa 143 and Psa 51 (the crushing chains); Judg 19 and the other merry-heart narratives (threshold states); 2Co 2 → 7 (the spirit's rest through persons); 2Ki 2 (spirit transfer confirmed by others); Meaning shifts with circumstance in consistent ways: *crush*: by whom, and turned to whom (§5); *tender heart*: to what it yields (§6); *good heart*: from God or from wine (§7); *love / hate one's soul*: well-being vs clinging (§3); *hāgâ*: what the heart rehearses (§12.2); *nûaḥ*: what rests in or on the person (§9.5); Inner states spread between people: the fainthearted soldier melts others (Deu 20:8); heart-speech is reported (Gen 27:42); a lowly heart gives rest to other souls (Mat 11:29); a congregation refreshes Titus's spirit (2Co 7:13); the prophet's heart takes in the people's doom (Jer 4:18–19); Other spirits relate to people as occupants of a house (Mat 12:43–45) and as seizures between people (1Sa 18:10; Judg 9:23 in Batch D). The divine Spirit rests upon people and is recognised by others (Num 11; 2Ki 2).; Fringe worth keeping: the knit soul beside the seizing spirit in one chapter (1Sa 18); the heart awake while the body lags (Song 5); God refusing to complete reciprocal abhorrence (Lev 26:44); Jezebel curing a vexed spirit by a manufactured good heart (1Ki 21); the prophet's heart for Moab set against Ammon's malice of soul (Isa 15; Jer 48; Eze 25); past hatred as a legal criterion (Deu 19)

17016.text: The merry heart made vulnerable by wine: "Nabal's heart was merry within him, for he was very drunk" (1Sa 25:36); "when Amnon's heart is merry with wine … strike Amnon" (2Sa 13:28); "when the heart of the king was merry with wine, he commanded" (Est 1:10); "when their hearts were merry, they said, 'Call Samson'" (Judg 16:25); [Claude reading] Four narratives in which a wine-merry heart is the moment of exposure or rash command.; Revisit 2026-09-28: with before/after context and five further instances (Judg 19:6, 9, 22; Rut 3:7; 1Ki 21:7; Luk 12:19), this is a threshold pattern. After food and wine the good heart lowers guard, and what enters at that moment decides the outcome: murder, anger, catastrophe, outrage, redemption (Ruth), a dead heart next morning (Nabal), God's claim on the soul (Luk 12:20). See Batch F §7.

17099.text: Recalling: "But this I call to mind [*heart*], and therefore I have hope" (Lam 3:21).

17100.text: 6.2 The soul addressed, and the soul speaking: [Claude reading] Hope is produced by an inner dialogue. The self speaks to its soul (Psa 42), the soul speaks back (Lam 3:24), and the heart recalls (Lam 3:21). This matches the "said in heart" material due in Batch E.

17102.text: 6.4 Hope and the NT inner seat: "my heart was glad … my flesh also will dwell in hope" (Act 2:26) — flesh in hope; "hope does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit" (Rom 5:5) [D1]; "by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope" (Rom 15:13) [D1]; "through the Spirit, by faith, we ourselves eagerly wait for the hope of righteousness" (Gal 5:5) [D3]; "one body and one Spirit … one hope" (Eph 4:4) [D1]; "the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope" (Eph 1:18); "in your hearts honor Christ … a reason for the hope that is in you" (1Pe 3:15); "waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him" (Luk 2:25) [D1]

17111.text: 7.2 The soul that seeks — longing in motion: "earnestly I seek you; my soul thirsts for you; my flesh faints for you" (Psa 63:1); "My soul yearns for you in the night; my spirit within me earnestly seeks you" (Isa 26:9) [H1]; "I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, but found him not" (Song 3:1–2); "My soul failed me when he spoke. I sought him, but found him not" (Song 5:6); "which my soul has sought repeatedly, but I have not found" (Ecc 7:28); "In the day of my trouble I seek the Lord … my soul refuses to be comforted" (Psa 77:2)

17145.text: 8.7 ◆ Spirits departing and returning: "the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and a harmful spirit from the Lord tormented him" (1Sa 16:14) [D1+O]; "Saul was refreshed … and the harmful spirit departed from him" (1Sa 16:23) [O]; "I will return to my house from which I came" (Luk 11:24) [O]; "Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit" (Luk 4:1) [D1] — travel, noted for the Spirit only; "by the breath of his mouth he will depart" (Job 15:30); "my beloved had turned and gone. My soul failed me" (Song 5:6)

17147.text: Promised end: "they shall no more stubbornly follow their own evil heart" (Jer 3:17)

17158.text: 9.4 Despising and rejecting — heart and soul as agents: "she despised him in her heart" (2Sa 6:16; 1Ch 15:29) — Michal; "How I hated discipline, and my heart despised reproof!" (Pro 5:12); "Whoever ignores instruction despises himself [*his nephesh*]" (Pro 15:32); "if your soul abhors my rules" (Lev 26:15); "their soul abhorred my statutes" (Lev 26:43); "the wicked … renounces God and says in his heart, 'You will not call to account'" (Psa 10:13; 10:3); "their heart went after their idols" (Eze 20:16)

17164.text: Deserted: "like a wife deserted and grieved in spirit … cast off" (Isa 54:6) [H1].

17194.text: Parted at death: dust to earth, spirit to God, soul to Sheol or delivered (Eccl 12:7; Gen 35:18).

17211.text: Inside one person, perplexity leads to a question, then waiting for an interpreter (Act 10:17-19).

17235.text: c. Inner speech — the heart as the place one "says" things: "Said in his heart / to himself": Gen 17:17; 24:45; 27:41; 1Ki 12:26; 1Sa 27:1; Deu 7:17; 8:17; 9:4; 18:21; Psa 10:6, 11, 13; 14:1; 53:1; Isa 14:13; 47:8, 10; 49:21; Jer 5:24; 13:22; Obd 3; Zep 1:12; 2:15; Est 6:6; Ecc 1:16; 2:1, 15; 3:17–18; Rom 10:6; Rev 18:7.; Hannah "was speaking in her heart; only her lips moved" (1Sa 1:13).; "Before I had finished speaking in my heart" (Gen 24:45).; The *content* of heart-speech is often self-assessment or self-deception: "I shall not be moved" (Psa 10:6); "There is no God" (Psa 14:1); "My power … has gotten me this wealth" (Deu 8:17); "I am, and there is no one besides me" (Isa 47:8; Zep 2:15).; Nehemiah "took counsel with *myself*" (Neh 5:7, lēv); "Ask *yourself*" style reflexives also appear.

17236.text: d. Thinking, planning, understanding, remembering: *Plans and devising:* Pro 16:1, 9; 19:21; 6:14, 18; 24:2; 12:20; Psa 140:2; 58:2; Zec 7:10; 8:17; Isa 10:7; Act 5:4; Eze 38:10.; *Understanding and knowing:*; "a heart to understand" (Deu 29:4); "understanding mind" (1Ki 3:9); "understand with their hearts" (Isa 6:10; Mat 13:15; Joh 12:40; Act 28:27); "an intelligent heart acquires knowledge" (Pro 18:15); "the heart of the hasty will understand" (Isa 32:4); *Remembering and "laying to heart":*; Isa 47:7; 57:1, 11; 42:25; Mal 2:2; Jer 12:11; Ecc 7:2; 9:1; Deu 4:39; 32:46; 1Sa 21:12; "call to mind" (Lam 3:21; Deu 30:1); "come into mind" (Jer 3:16; 7:31; 19:5; 32:35; 44:21; 51:50; Isa 65:17); Haggai's repeated "Consider your ways" is literally *set your heart* (Hag 1:5, 7; 2:15, 18) [lexical].; *Searching and investigating:* "I applied my heart to seek and to search out" (Ecc 1:13, 17; 7:25; 8:9, 16); "great searchings of heart" (Judg 5:15–16).; *Pondering and treasuring:* Mary "treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart" (Luk 2:19, 51); "ponder in your own hearts on your beds" (Psa 4:4); "the meditation of my heart" (Psa 19:14; 49:3).; *Questioning and reasoning:* Mar 2:6, 8; Luk 3:15; 5:22; 9:47; 24:38.

17237.text: e. Willing, deciding, purposing, being moved: *Deciding:*; "Daniel resolved" (Dan 1:8); "Joash decided" (2Ch 24:4); "has determined this in his heart" (1Co 7:37); "Each one must give as he has decided in his heart" (2Co 9:7); "of my own will / accord" (Num 24:13; 16:28, lēv); "It is in my heart to make a covenant" (2Ch 29:10); "I had it in my heart to build a house" (1Ch 22:7; 28:2; 1Ki 8:17–18); *Being moved to give:* "everyone whose heart stirred him … and everyone whose spirit moved him" (Exo 35:21); also Exo 25:2; 35:5, 22, 26, 29; 36:2; 2Ki 12:4 ("the money that a man's heart prompts him to bring").; *Intention as depth:* "The purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out" (Pro 20:5); "the inward mind and heart of a man are deep" (Psa 64:6).

17238.text: f. Feeling: *Joy and gladness:* 1Ki 8:66; Pro 15:13, 15; 27:9, 11; Psa 4:7; 13:5; 16:9; 19:8; 28:7; 33:21; Zep 3:14; Joh 16:22.; *Merriment with wine:* Est 1:10; 2Sa 13:28; Rut 3:7; Judg 16:25; 19:6, 22.; *Sorrow and anguish:* Neh 2:2; Rom 9:2; 2Co 2:4; Joh 16:6; Psa 13:2; 55:4; Lam 1:20; 5:15.; *Fear and melting:* Gen 42:28; 1Sa 28:5; Deu 20:3, 8; Jos 7:5; Isa 7:2; 13:7; 21:4; 35:4; Jer 4:9; Nah 2:10.; *Courage:* Psa 27:14; 31:24; 2Sa 7:27; 17:10; Eze 22:14; Amo 2:16; Psa 76:5; plus the NT compounds "take heart" (Mat 9:2, 22; 14:27; Mar 6:50; 10:49; Joh 16:33; Act 23:11) and "lose heart" (Luk 18:1; 2Co 4:1, 16; Eph 3:13; Gal 6:9; 2Th 3:13).; *Desire:* "the desires of your heart" (Psa 37:4); "heart's desire" (Psa 21:2; 20:4; Rom 10:1).; *Love, attachment, contempt, hate:*; "the king's heart went out to Absalom" (2Sa 14:1); "my heart goes out to the commanders" (Judg 5:9); "your heart is not with me" (Judg 16:15); "I hold you in my heart" (Phili 1:7); "you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together" (2Co 7:3); "despised him in her heart" (2Sa 6:16); "You shall not hate your brother in your heart" (Lev 19:17); *Grief felt in the heart as physical pain:* "My anguish, my anguish! I writhe in pain! Oh the walls of my heart! My heart is beating wildly" (Jer 4:19); "My heart throbs" (Psa 38:10); "my heart is like wax; it is melted within my breast" (Psa 22:14).

17242.text: j. The heart's own "senses": fringe: "having the eyes of your hearts enlightened" (Eph 1:18); "God … has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge" (2Co 4:6); "until … the morning star rises in your hearts" (2Pe 1:19); "a veil lies over their hearts" (2Co 3:15).; fringe: "I slept, but my heart was awake" (Song 5:2); "Even in the night his heart does not rest" (Ecc 2:23).

17246.text: n. Heart and "mind": *ESV renders lēv as "mind":* 1Ki 3:9, 12; 4:29; 10:24; Pro 19:21; 28:26; Jer 14:14; 23:16; Lam 3:21; Neh 4:6; 6:8; 2Ki 6:11.; *Aramaic lēvav (H3825) is mostly "mind":* Dan 2:30; 4:16; 5:21; 7:4.; *Pairs in the text:* "test the heart and the mind" (Jer 11:20; 17:10; 20:12; Psa 26:2; 7:9; Rev 2:23); "hearts and … minds" (Phili 4:7); law "into their minds … on their hearts" / "on their hearts … on their minds" (Heb 8:10 / 10:16).; [lexical; verify] In several "heart and mind" pairs, the ESV "heart" may translate *kilyah* (kidneys) or the reverse. The CSV tags only the M47 word, so which English word carries the M47 tag varies (e.g. Jer 11:20, where the M47 tag sits on "mind").; fringe: a human heart/mind can be exchanged for a beast's and back: "let his mind be changed from a man's, and let a beast's mind be given to him" (Dan 4:16; 5:21); a beast is "given the mind of a man" (Dan 7:4).

17257.text: c. What is done to the soul: *Hunted, pursued, torn:* Eze 13:18–20 ("hunt the souls like birds"); Psa 7:2, 5; 143:3; 57:4.; *Delivered, redeemed, ransomed, kept:* Psa 116:4, 8; 49:15; 55:18; 86:13; 1Ki 1:29; Psa 25:20; 121:7.; *Restored, revived:* "He restores my soul" (Psa 23:3); "The law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul" (Psa 19:7).; *Nourished by words:*; "Gracious words … sweetness to the soul and health to the body" (Pro 16:24); "Like cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news" (Pro 25:25); a faithful messenger "refreshes the soul" (Pro 25:13); wisdom "life for your soul" (Pro 3:22; 24:14); *NT:*; "passions of the flesh, which wage war against your soul" (1Pe 2:11); "Having purified your souls by your obedience to the truth" (1Pe 1:22); "the implanted word, which is able to save your souls" (Jam 1:21); "anchor of the soul" (Heb 6:19); "they entice unsteady souls" (2Pe 2:14); "unsettling your minds / poisoned their minds" (psychē, Act 15:24; 14:2)

17258.text: d. Soul and death: "as her soul was departing (for she was dying)" (Gen 35:18); "you will not abandon my soul to Sheol" (Psa 16:10; Act 2:27); "brought up my soul from Sheol" (Psa 30:3); soul // life near the pit (Job 33:18, 22, 28, 30); "my soul would soon have lived in the land of silence" (Psa 94:17); "This night your soul is required of you" (Luk 12:20); "forfeit his soul" (Mat 16:26; Mar 8:36–37); "do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul" (Mat 10:28); "the souls of those who had been slain" under the altar (Rev 6:9; 20:4)

17260.text: b. The human spirit: *Troubled, anxious:* Gen 41:8; Dan 2:1, 3; 7:15 ("my spirit within me was anxious, and the visions of my head alarmed me"); Joh 13:21; 2Co 2:13.; *Revived:*; after eating ("his spirit revived" 1Sa 30:12); after drinking ("his spirit returned, and he revived" Judg 15:19); on good news (Gen 45:27); *Broken, crushed:* Exo 6:9 ("broken spirit and harsh slavery"); Pro 15:4, 13; 17:22; 18:14 ("A man's spirit will endure sickness, but a crushed spirit who can bear?"); Job 17:1; Psa 34:18; 51:17.; *Faint, failing:* Psa 77:3; 142:3; 143:4, 7; Isa 57:16; 61:3.; *Lowly, contrite vs proud, haughty:* Isa 57:15; 66:2; Pro 16:18–19; 29:23; Ecc 7:8; Mat 5:3 ("poor in spirit").; *Governed or ungoverned:* "he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city" (Pro 16:32); "Be not quick in your spirit to become angry" (Ecc 7:9).; *Weighed by God:* "the Lord weighs the spirit" (Pro 16:2).; *Knowing and understanding:*; "it is the spirit in man, the breath of the Almighty, that makes him understand" (Job 32:8); "out of my understanding a spirit answers me" (Job 20:3); "the spirit within me constrains me" (Job 32:18); "who knows a person's thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him?" (1Co 2:11) — [Claude reading] the spirit as the person's self-knowledge.; *Distinct from "mind" (nous) in prayer:* "my spirit prays but my mind is unfruitful … I will pray with my spirit, but I will pray with my mind also" (1Co 14:14–15); "be renewed in the spirit of your minds" (Eph 4:23).; *Jesus' spirit:* "perceiving in his spirit" (Mar 2:8); "sighed deeply in his spirit" (Mar 8:12); "deeply moved in his spirit" (Joh 11:33); "troubled in his spirit" (Joh 13:21); "yielded up his spirit" (Mat 27:50; Joh 19:30; Luk 23:46).; *Paul's spirit:* "his spirit was provoked within him" (Act 17:16); "my spirit was not at rest" (2Co 2:13); "refreshed my spirit" (1Co 16:18); "I serve with my spirit" (Rom 1:9).; *Fervent:* "fervent in spirit" (Rom 12:11; Act 18:25); "grew and became strong in spirit" (Luk 1:80).; *Stirred by God:*; "the Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus" (2Ch 36:22; Ezr 1:1); "everyone whose spirit God had stirred" (Ezr 1:5); the spirit of Zerubbabel (Hag 1:14); of Pul (1Ch 5:26); of the Medes (Jer 51:11); *Hardened by God:* "the Lord your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate" (Deu 2:30).

17276.text: 3.6 Cause and effect between inner seat, body and senses: *Heart → spirit:* "by sorrow of heart the spirit is crushed" (Pro 15:13).; *Heart / spirit → body, face, bones:*; "A glad heart makes a cheerful face" (Pro 15:13); "A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot" (Pro 14:30); "A joyful heart is good medicine, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones" (Pro 17:22); "a trembling heart and failing eyes and a languishing soul" (Deu 28:65); "My heart throbs; my strength fails me, and the light of my eyes — it also has gone" (Psa 38:10); "Every heart will melt, and all hands will be feeble; every spirit will faint, and all knees will be weak as water" (Eze 21:7); "Hearts melt and knees tremble; anguish is in all loins; all faces grow pale" (Nah 2:10); "My heart is struck down like grass … I forget to eat my bread" (Psa 102:4); "My heart is broken within me; all my bones shake" (Jer 23:9); "your heart shall rejoice; your bones shall flourish like the grass" (Isa 66:14); "For this our heart has become sick, for these things our eyes have grown dim" (Lam 5:17); "my stomach churns; my heart is wrung within me" (Lam 1:20); *Body / face / senses → heart:*; "by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (Ecc 7:3); "The light of the eyes rejoices the heart, and good news refreshes the bones" (Pro 15:30); "my heart has gone after my eyes" (Job 31:7); "not to follow after your own heart and your own eyes" (Num 15:39); "everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart" (Mat 5:28); *Food and drink → heart / spirit / soul:*; "Strengthen your heart with a morsel of bread" (Judg 19:5, 8); "wine to gladden the heart of man … bread to strengthen man's heart" (Psa 104:15); "satisfying your hearts with food and gladness" (Act 14:17); "when he had eaten, his spirit revived" (1Sa 30:12); "when he drank, his spirit returned" (Judg 15:19); "when the wine had gone out of Nabal … his heart died within him, and he became as a stone" (1Sa 25:37); "it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace, not by foods" (Heb 13:9); "Oil and perfume make the heart glad" (Pro 27:9); *Fasting afflicts the soul:* Psa 35:13 ("I afflicted myself [nephesh] with fasting"); Psa 69:10; Isa 58:3, 5; the Day of Atonement "afflict yourselves" (Lev 16:29–31; 23:27–32; Num 29:7).

Soul-states, spirit, God's Spirit, words, law and dispositions are placed "in" it. Spirit and soul are also spoken of as "within me", but they are less often described as containers.

17280.text: 3.9 The boundary of death — where the components come apart: *Soul departs:* "as her soul was departing" (Gen 35:18); soul to Sheol, pit, silence (§2.2d).; *Spirit and breath return to God:*; "the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it" (Ecc 12:7); "Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward and the spirit of the beast goes down into the earth?" (Ecc 3:21); "When you take away their breath, they die and return to their dust" (Psa 104:29); "Into your hand I commit my spirit" (Psa 31:5; Luk 23:46; Act 7:59); "No man has power to retain the spirit" (Ecc 8:8); *Return to life:*; "her spirit returned, and she got up" (Luk 8:55); "the life of the child came into him again, and he revived" (1Ki 17:21–22), with "the flesh of the child became warm" (2Ki 4:34); "a breath of life from God entered them" (Rev 11:11); Ezekiel 37: flesh, sinews, skin → breath → life; *Life in the blood:* "the life [nephesh] of the flesh is in the blood" (Lev 17:11, 14; Gen 9:4–5; Deu 12:23).; *Body without spirit:* "the body apart from the spirit is dead" (Jam 2:26).; *Dead body = nephesh:* H5315M (Num 19:11, 13).; *Beyond death:* "the spirits of the righteous made perfect" (Heb 12:23); "the spirits in prison" (1Pe 3:19); "the souls … under the altar" (Rev 6:9).; *Plans perish when breath departs:* Psa 146:4.; [Claude reading] Death is where the text most clearly *separates* the terms: flesh/dust goes to the earth; spirit/breath goes to God; soul goes to Sheol, or is delivered; the blood carries the life; In ordinary life the same terms overlap and stand in for one another.

18368.text: The soul is said to die. "Let me die the death of the upright, and let my end be like his!" "Let me die with the Philistines." In both, the Hebrew is *let my soul die*. "Behold, all souls are mine … the soul who sins shall die." Elijah "asked that he might die" (literally, asked for his soul to die), and so did Jonah.

18372.text: Q2 (soul and spirit at death). The verses give the soul more than one face at death. It departs (Gen 35:18). It dies (Num 23:10; Eze 18:4). It is poured out to death (Isa 53:12). It goes to the generation of its fathers (Psa 49:19). It is ransomed from Sheol's power, "for he will receive me" (Psa 49:15). It is not abandoned to Sheol, which Peter reads of Christ (Act 2:27, 31). Of the spirit, they say it is committed, taken, or returns to God (Luk 23:46; Psa 104:29; Ecc 12:7); "who knows" where it goes (Ecc 3:21); and the dead "live in the spirit the way God does" (1Pe 4:6). No verse sends the soul one way and the spirit another. These are set side by side, unreconciled.

18877.text: Hiding from God: In each scene where a person hides from God, something of God is perceived first: a sound (Genesis 3:10), God naming himself (Exodus 3:6), "the terror of the Lord, and … the splendor of his majesty" (Isaiah 2:10), "the face of him who is seated on the throne, and … the wrath of the Lamb" (Revelation 6:16).; Adam hid because he knew he was naked (Genesis 3:10).; Moses "hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God" (Exodus 3:6), and no wrong is named.; At the end, people call "to the mountains and rocks, 'Fall on us and hide us'", for "who can stand?" (Revelation 6:16–17).; Job names the one condition on which he will not hide: "Only grant me two things, then I will not hide myself from your face: withdraw your hand far from me, and let not dread of you terrify me" (Job 13:20–21). In his words, it is the dread that makes a person hide.; None of it works. "Can a man hide himself in secret places so that I cannot see him? declares the Lord. Do I not fill heaven and earth?" (Jeremiah 23:24). "There is no gloom or deep darkness where evildoers may hide themselves" (Job 34:22). Isaiah names what the attempt does: "Ah, you who hide deep from the Lord your counsel … and who say, 'Who sees us? Who knows us?' You turn things upside down! Shall the potter be regarded as the clay" (Isaiah 29:15–16).; That nothing is hidden from God is the same fact for everyone, and it falls very differently.; For the one who suffers it is comfort: "O Lord, all my longing is before you; my sighing is not hidden from you" (Psalm 38:9).; For the one being made it is wonder: "My frame was not hidden from you, when I was being made in secret" (Psalm 139:15), and the psalmist answers, "my soul knows it very well" (139:14).; For the one who has done wrong it is judgement: "I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me; for now, O Ephraim, you have played the whore" (Hosea 5:3).

19188.text: What it does. It puts a covering between the self and God: "among the trees of the garden" (Gen 3:8); "Moses hid his face" (Exo 3:6); "enter into the rock and hide in the dust" (Isa 2:10); "in the caves and among the rocks … Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne" (Rev 6:15–16)

19189.text: Where it comes from. In every case a perception of God comes first: "I heard the sound of you in the garden" (Gen 3:10); God names himself: "I am the God of your father" (Exo 3:6); "the terror of the Lord, and … the splendor of his majesty" (Isa 2:10); "the face of him who is seated on the throne, and … the wrath of the Lamb" (Rev 6:16); Inside the person, what meets that perception differs: Adam: knowledge of exposure. "The eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked" (Gen 3:7), and so "I was afraid, because I was naked" (3:10).; Moses: "he was afraid to look at God" (Exo 3:6), with no transgression stated.; The kings, the great, "slave and free": "who can stand?" (Rev 6:17).

19190.text: How it co-exists. It is always with fear (Gen 3:10; Exo 3:6), terror (Isa 2:10), or wrath felt as unbearable (Rev 6:16–17). In Adam, self-knowledge ("naked") comes between perception and fear. Job 13:20–22 turns the phenomenon inside out. Job names the conditions under which he will *not* hide: "withdraw your hand far from me, and let not dread of you terrify me. Then call, and I will answer". Job shows that hiding is what dread produces. Remove the dread and the person can face God and speak.

19191.text: What it leads to. The same act has three outcomes: Being sought and questioned: "Where are you?" (Gen 3:9), then Adam's answer and his blame of the woman (3:12); Being addressed further: God goes on to speak to the hidden-faced Moses, "I have surely seen the affliction of my people" (Exo 3:7); Despair of standing at all (Rev 6:17)

19212.text: What it does in the human: Dismay: "you hid your face; I was dismayed" (Psa 30:7); "When you hide your face, they are dismayed; when you take away their breath, they die" (Psa 104:29); The spirit failing: "My spirit fails! Hide not your face from me, lest I be like those who go down to the pit" (Psa 143:7); Being cast away: "why do you cast my soul away? Why do you hide your face" (Psa 88:14); Feeling forgotten: "Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?" (Psa 13:1). The seat follows at once: "How long must I take counsel in my soul and have sorrow in my heart all the day?" (13:2); The body pressed down: "Why do you hide your face? … For our soul is bowed down to the dust; our belly clings to the ground" (Psa 44:24–25); Melting: "you have hidden your face from us, and have made us melt in the hand of our iniquities" (Isa 64:7). The previous verse: "We all fade like a leaf" (64:6); Being counted an enemy: "Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy?" (Job 13:24); "Will you frighten a driven leaf?" (13:25); A collective conclusion: "Have not these evils come upon us because our God is not among us?" (Deu 31:17); Complaint: "My way is hidden from the Lord, and my right is disregarded by my God" (Isa 40:27). The answer: "He does not faint or grow weary … He gives power to the faint" (40:28–29); Banishment and the fear that follows it: Cain, "from your face I shall be hidden. I shall be a fugitive … whoever finds me will kill me" (Gen 4:14), after "My punishment is greater than I can bear" (4:13). Being hidden from God's face is followed at once by fear of man.

19217.text: Psa 51:9 → 51:10 "Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me". New in v3: when God is asked to hide his face *from the sin*, the next request places the remedy in the heart and spirit. The seat is where the cleansing is to happen. The requests go on: "Cast me not away from your presence, and take not your Holy Spirit from me" (51:11), then "uphold me with a willing spirit" (51:12). The face hidden from the sin (51:9) is set against the presence not withdrawn from the person (51:11). Between them stand two spirits: God's, which is not to be taken away, and the human's, which is to be renewed and made willing.; New in v3: Psa 102:2 ("Do not hide your face from me in the day of my distress") → 102:4 "My heart is struck down like grass and has withered; I forget to eat my bread". The distress of 102:2 is a withered heart, and it reaches the body: the sufferer forgets to eat. It is the same movement as Psa 44:25 ("our belly clings to the ground").; New in v3: Psa 27:9 ← 27:8 "You have said, 'Seek my face.' My heart says to you, 'Your face, Lord, do I seek.'" The heart seeks the face one verse before it asks that the face not be hidden. The petition "Hide not your face" (27:9) is the voice of a heart already turned toward the face. What hiddenness would cut off is the heart's own seeking.; New in v3: Psa 69:17 → 69:20 "Reproaches have broken my heart, so that I am in despair. I looked for pity, but there was none". The "distress" of 69:17 is named three verses later as a broken heart that finds no comforter. The hidden face of 69:17 and the absent human pity of 69:20 are the same lack, felt from God and from people. In between, the petition names the soul: "Draw near to my soul, redeem me" (69:18). The opposite of the hidden face is God drawing near to the soul.; New in v3, the resolution in the heart: Psa 22:24 ("he has not hidden his face from him, but has heard") → 22:26 "The afflicted shall eat and be satisfied; those who seek him shall praise the Lord! May your hearts live forever!" When the face is not hidden, the outcome lands in hearts that live. It is the reverse of the withered heart that forgets to eat (Psa 102:4): here the afflicted eat, and the hearts live.

19218.text: Life-sense, in the passage: Psa 89:46 ("How long, O Lord? Will you hide yourself forever?") → 89:48 "What man can live and never see death? Who can deliver his soul from the power of Sheol?" *Nephesh* here is the life facing death. The hidden face is set against human mortality. This is a pointer to Batch G v3 §16.4 ("The soul delivered from death"), not read further here.; New in v3: Isa 54:8 ← 54:6 "the Lord has called you like a wife deserted and grieved in spirit, like a wife of youth when she is cast off". The momentary hiding of 54:8 is borne in a grieved spirit (the bearer's own, Zion's). The image is marital: the hidden face is felt as desertion.; Spurious context links: Isa 64:7 ← 64:6 "our iniquities, like the wind, take us away" (*ruach* as wind); Mic 3:4 ← 3:2–3 "flesh" (the flesh torn from the people). Neither is an inner seat.; What the map shows. Every genuine seat in this phenomenon falls on the human side. Three forms: The sufferer's spirit, soul or heart is where the hiddenness is felt: failing, cast away, sorrowing, bowed down, broken, grieved.; The offender's heart is where it is misread or ignored: "God has forgotten" (Psa 10:11); "the way of his own heart" (Isa 57:17).; God's Spirit is where it ends: poured out (Eze 39:29).

19230.text: How it co-exists. Fear is the most frequent companion, on both sides: fear drives concealment (Job 31:34; Mat 25:25), or follows its failure (Exo 2:14); fear blocks disclosure until it is overcome (1Sa 3:15–18); Joy (Mat 13:44), enjoyment of sin (Job 20:12–13) and conscience (2Ki 7:9) are the other companions.

19240.text: What it leads to. Mostly, something from outside ends it: "While they were perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them" (Luk 24:4); "the men … stood at the gate" and "the Spirit said to him" (Act 10:17, 19); "Peter, standing with the eleven, lifted up his voice" (Act 2:14); the queen names Daniel (Dan 5:10–12); Herod "sought to see him" (Luk 9:9); Perplexity ends when an interpreter or a meeting arrives.

19342.text: What the map shows across the phenomena.: Where the genuine seats fall: on the one who suffers the phenomenon (FH, AX, TR, LH); on the one who causes or misreads it (FH, CD, and in context TR and LH); on an interpreter or diagnoser (PX Dan 5:12, UC Luk 9:47, both in context); The concealment phenomena that are outward acts (HG, HS, SH) have no genuine seat in-verse at all. In context, their nearest seat word is the life that is hunted (Psa 54:4) or the heart that melted into confession (Jos 2:11).; The seat word does four jobs in M20, and only one is "where the phenomenon sits": the location (Pro 12:25; Psa 143:7); the object (Mat 6:25; 1Cor 7:34); the landing place of the answer (Psa 94:19; Phili 4:7); the site of the remedy (Jam 4:8; Psa 51:10); The seat often comes one verse away, and the direction matters: before the phenomenon, as its cause or ground (Psa 27:8; Deu 1:28; Isa 29:13; Isa 54:6; Dan 11:27); after it, as its experience, its diagnosis, or its answer (Psa 13:2; 69:20; 102:4; Luk 9:47; Phili 4:7; Psa 31:5–7; 35:9; 22:26); The seat of the one who does *not* undergo the phenomenon sometimes stands beside it: Caleb's "different spirit" among the grumblers (Num 14:24); the prudent one who "guards his soul" (Pro 22:5); Daniel's "excellent spirit" among the perplexed (Dan 5:12). The seat is named in the contrast figure, not in the crowd.; Concealment of the heart behind speech or act recurs outside §7: the trapper's heart (Psa 64:6; 140:2), the whisperer's glazed lips over an evil heart (Pro 26:23, 25), the aggressor's heart set before the act (Dan 11:28). In these phenomena the hidden thing is the heart itself.
